How to use this book

  1. Print it on A4 and keep it in a folder, away from damp. Paper works when there is no power.
  2. Each page is one skill: why it matters, what you need, the steps and a drawing with numbers ①②③.
  3. The dots ●○○ show difficulty: ● easy for anyone, ●● needs some practice, ●●● needs patience and skill.
  4. Practise the skills NOW, while all is well. An emergency is not the time to try for the first time.
  5. Teach them to your children and grandchildren. Knowledge passed from hand to hand is never lost.
⚠ These instructions are general information, not medical or professional advice. Always read the warnings. For serious health problems see a doctor or pharmacist. Follow your local laws (fishing, plant gathering, open fires). The author accepts no liability for misuse.

Chapter 1

Water & Hygiene

Clean water and hygiene save more lives than any medicine. Here you will learn how to collect water, how to clean it so it is safe to drink, and how to store it. And how to keep a home clean and healthy, without sewers or power.

💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.1

Collecting rainwater from the roof

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon
① gutter ② mesh on the inlet ③ downpipe ④ closed barrel ⑤ tap above the sludge ⑥ overflow to the garden
Why: If the tap water stops, your roof becomes a spring. 10 mm of rain on a 50 m² roof gives about 500 litres.
What you need
  • gutter and downpipe
  • barrel with lid, dark colour
  • fine mesh screen
  • barrel tap
  • bricks or concrete blocks
Step by step
  1. Clean leaves and dirt from the roof and the gutter.
  2. Set the barrel up on bricks, high enough for a bucket under the tap.
  3. Fit the tap 5 cm above the bottom, so the sludge stays below.
  4. Run the pipe from the gutter to the barrel lid.
  5. Put mesh over the inlet, against leaves and mosquitoes.
  6. Make an overflow hole near the top, with a pipe to the garden.
  7. Keep the barrel always closed and out of the sun.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Several barrels can be joined with a pipe at the bottom. They fill together.
⚠ Careful: Rainwater is NOT safe to drink as it is. Boil or disinfect it first. Do not collect from roofs with asbestos sheets, tar or old lead paint.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.2

First-flush diverter

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2 hours
① water from the gutter ② T-piece ③ chamber with the dirty first water ④ ball rises and seals ⑤ clean water to the barrel ⑥ cap with tiny drain hole
Why: The first rain washes dust, bird droppings and leaves off the roof. We throw away this small dirty part and keep the clean water.
What you need
  • plastic pipe 10 cm wide (1–2 m)
  • T-piece of the same size
  • screw-on end cap
  • small floating ball
  • reducer (narrowing) for the ball
  • pipe glue
Step by step
  1. Allow 1 litre of first water for each m² of roof.
  2. One metre of 10 cm pipe holds about 8 litres. Cut the length you need.
  3. Fit the T-piece in the downpipe. The side outlet goes to the barrel.
  4. Glue the upright pipe (the 'chamber') below it.
  5. Drop in the ball. Fit the narrowing on top, so the ball can seal it.
  6. Close the bottom with a screw cap. Drill a 2 mm hole in it.
  7. The chamber fills, the ball rises and seals. The rest flows to the barrel.
  8. After each rain, unscrew the cap and empty the sludge.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The tiny hole slowly empties the chamber by itself, ready for the next rain.
⚠ Careful: Even after the diverter, the water must be boiled or disinfected before drinking.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.3

Bucket filter with gravel, sand and charcoal

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 3 hours + 2 weeks to 'ripen'
① plate with holes (under some water) ② fine sand ③ charcoal ④ coarse sand ⑤ gravel ⑥ small tap ⑦ clean pot — then boil it!
Why: The water passes through gravel, sand and charcoal. They hold back the mud, the dirt and many germs, like a strainer. So cloudy water comes out clear. CAREFUL: clear does not mean safe. Always boil it or add bleach after.
What you need
  • big plastic bucket
  • small tap
  • washed gravel
  • washed coarse and fine sand
  • charcoal from a wood fire
  • plate with holes, or cloth
Step by step
  1. Drill a hole in the side, 3 cm from the bottom, and fit the tap.
  2. Wash the sand and gravel until the water runs clear.
  3. Put 5 cm of gravel at the bottom, covering the tap.
  4. Add 5 cm of coarse sand.
  5. Add 5 cm of washed charcoal, broken to rice size.
  6. Add 15 cm of fine sand on top.
  7. Lay a plate with holes on top, so water does not dig the sand.
  8. Pour water in gently. Collect from the tap in a clean pot.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: In the first 2 weeks a slimy 'skin' forms on the sand that traps germs. Do not stir it.
⚠ Careful: Filtered does not mean safe! Always boil, bleach or sun-treat after. Do not use barbecue briquettes with chemicals.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.4

Boiling: the safest water

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes
① strain through cloth ② rolling boil ③ 1 minute (3 in high mountains) ④ fire ⑤ covered clean container
Why: Boiling kills bacteria, parasites and viruses. You only need a fire and a pot.
What you need
  • clean cotton cloth
  • pot with a lid
  • fire or camping stove
  • clean container with a lid
Step by step
  1. Let cloudy water settle for 1 hour.
  2. Strain it through a folded cloth into the pot.
  3. Bring it to a strong, rolling boil.
  4. Keep it boiling 1 minute. Above 2,000 m altitude, 3 minutes.
  5. Cover it and let it cool.
  6. Pour it into a clean container and close it.
  7. To remove the 'flat' taste, pour it from one pot to another a few times.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Old-timers added a pinch of salt to boiled water for a better taste.
⚠ Careful: Boiling does NOT remove chemicals, fuel or salt. Watch out for burns; keep children away. Never use a fire or stove indoors without air (carbon monoxide).
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.5

Sun disinfection in bottles (SODIS)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 6 hours of sun
① clear bottle lying flat ② 6 hours of sun ③ metal sheet on bricks ④ fill 3/4, shake, then fill to the top
Why: Sunlight kills germs inside clear bottles. Free, with no fuel.
What you need
  • clear plastic PET bottles, up to 2 litres
  • metal sheet or sunny flat roof
  • clear water (not cloudy)
Step by step
  1. Wash the bottles. Remove the labels.
  2. Test: stand the full bottle on a newspaper. If you cannot read the big headline, filter first.
  3. Fill 3/4, close and shake hard for 20 seconds.
  4. Fill to the top and close.
  5. Lay the bottles flat on a metal sheet, in the sun.
  6. Leave them 6 hours in sun. If very cloudy, 2 days.
  7. Drink straight from the bottle.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A metal sheet reflects sunlight and adds heat. It works even better.
⚠ Careful: NOT in continuous rain. NOT glass or coloured bottles. Replace old, dull or scratched bottles. It does not remove chemicals.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.6

Disinfecting water with bleach

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① plain unscented bleach ② dropper: 2 drops per litre ③ 1-litre jar ④ stir and cover ⑤ wait 30 minutes
Why: A few drops of bleach make many litres of water safe, with no fire.
What you need
  • plain bleach 4–6%, unscented
  • dropper
  • clean container with a lid
  • spoon
Step by step
  1. Read the label: only plain bleach, no scent or other additives.
  2. If the water is cloudy, strain it through a cloth first.
  3. Add 2 drops for each litre of clear water.
  4. If the water is cloudy or very cold, add 4 drops per litre.
  5. Stir and cover.
  6. Wait 30 minutes.
  7. Smell it: it should smell slightly of bleach. If not, add the same dose again and wait 15 minutes.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: For 20 litres (one jerrycan) you need 40 drops ≈ ½ teaspoon.
⚠ Careful: NEVER scented, thick or colour-safe bleach. Never mix bleach with vinegar or ammonia (toxic gas). Bleach older than 1 year loses strength. Keep away from children.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.7

Finding water in nature

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: as long as the walk
① low point of the valley ② green trees and reeds ③ animal paths joining ④ birds and bees ⑤ dig at the outside of the bend
Why: Nature shows where water hides. You only need to know how to look.
What you need
  • open eyes
  • small shovel or strong stick
  • container and cloth
Step by step
  1. Head downhill: ravines, gullies, the foot of mountains.
  2. Look for green trees and plants: plane trees, willows, reeds, brambles, fig trees.
  3. Follow animal paths downhill, where they join together.
  4. Watch bees, wasps and flies. They fly near water.
  5. Sparrows and pigeons fly low towards water, morning and evening.
  6. In a dry stream, dig at the outside of the bend.
  7. Dig 30–60 cm. If the soil is wet, wait for water to gather.
  8. Always strain and boil any water you find.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: In Greece, oleander and plane trees almost always mean water underground.
⚠ Careful: Oleander is POISONOUS — do not eat it or cook over its wood. Never camp in a dry stream bed: flash floods come suddenly. Avoid water near sprayed fields, mines or dead animals.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.8

Solar still and plant bag

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour to set up, 1 day to wait
① clear plastic sheet ② small stone in the middle ③ cup ④ green plants or wet soil ⑤ drinking tube ⑥ bag on a leafy branch ⑦ water gathers in the low corner
Why: In great need they give a little clean water. Not much, but it can keep you going.
What you need
  • clear plastic sheet 1.5×1.5 m
  • cup
  • stones
  • thin tube (straw) 1 m
  • clear plastic bag and string
Step by step
  1. Dig a hole 1 m wide and 60 cm deep, in a sunny place.
  2. Put the cup in the middle of the bottom.
  3. Put green leaves or wet soil around it. You can also pour salty or dirty water in (not into the cup).
  4. Cover with the plastic and fix the edges with stones and soil.
  5. Place a small stone in the middle, right above the cup.
  6. Run the tube from the cup to the outside, so you can drink without opening it.
  7. Bag: tie it over a leafy branch in the sun. Put a pebble in the low corner.
  8. In the evening, collect the water from the corner.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Dig in the morning or evening, when it is cool. Sweat costs you water.
⚠ Careful: It gives little: usually half a glass to 1 litre a day. Do not bag poisonous plants (oleander, spurge). Never drink seawater directly.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.9

Storing water at home

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 morning
① closed food-safe container ② label with date ③ on wood, not concrete ④ dark cool cupboard ⑤ 4 litres per person per day ⑥ use the oldest first, put new at the back
Why: We last only 3 days without water. A stock at home keeps you calm until you find another way.
What you need
  • food-safe jerrycans or bottles, with caps
  • masking tape and marker
  • pallet or wooden boards
  • unscented bleach
Step by step
  1. Allow 4 litres per person per day (drinking and cooking).
  2. Keep 2 weeks' worth if you can. For 4 people: 4 × 4 × 14 = 224 litres.
  3. Use only food-safe containers. No chemical or milk containers.
  4. Wash containers with soap and rinse with a little bleach.
  5. Fill from the tap and close tightly.
  6. Write the date on it.
  7. Keep them in a cool dark place, on wood, not on concrete.
  8. Every 6 months, water the garden with the old and refill fresh.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Remember water you already have: the water heater, toilet tank (not for drinking without boiling), canned food.
⚠ Careful: Keep away from petrol, pesticides and chemicals: plastic absorbs fumes. Do not use containers over 20 litres if you cannot lift them (20 kg).
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.10

Re-using grey water

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: every day
① wash in a basin ② bucket collects the water ③ pour quickly into the toilet bowl ④ water tree roots, not leaves
Why: Water from washing hands, dishes and clothes ('grey water') can water trees and flush the toilet. This saves your clean water.
What you need
  • basin in the sink
  • buckets
  • plain natural soap
Step by step
  1. Wash in a basin, not under running water.
  2. Empty the basin into a bucket.
  3. For the toilet: pour 5–8 litres quickly, straight into the toilet bowl.
  4. For the garden: pour onto the soil at the roots of trees and bushes.
  5. Put straw or leaves at the roots. The water soaks in and does not smell.
  6. Use it the same day. Do not store it.
  7. Change the watering spot every few days.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: With less soap, and plain soap (olive oil soap), plants cope better.
⚠ Careful: NOT on vegetables eaten raw. NOT water with bleach, grease, nappies or faeces (that is 'black water'). Keep away from wells.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.11

Bucket toilet with sawdust

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① lid ② seat ③ layers of sawdust over each use ④ sawdust bucket and scoop ⑤ compost heap covered with straw
Why: When the sewer or water stops, a bucket with sawdust keeps the house clean and free of smell.
What you need
  • 20-litre bucket with a lid
  • toilet seat or board with a hole
  • sawdust, dry leaves or ash
  • second bucket and a scoop
  • gloves
Step by step
  1. Put 5 cm of sawdust in the bottom of the bucket.
  2. Put the seat on top.
  3. After each use, cover with 1–2 scoops of sawdust. Nothing should show.
  4. Always close the lid.
  5. If you can, pee separately in another container. It smells much less.
  6. When it is 3/4 full, empty it onto a compost heap far from water.
  7. Cover the heap with straw or soil.
  8. Wash your hands well with soap.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Ash from the fireplace cuts the smell and keeps flies away.
⚠ Careful: The heap needs 1–2 years to become soil. Then use it only for trees, not vegetables. At least 30 m from wells. Always gloves and soap: cholera and diarrhoea spread from here.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.12

Simple pit latrine

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 day
① depth 1–1.5 m ② strong boards ③ lid on the hole ④ ash or soil after each use ⑤ at least 30 m from a well ⑥ wall of cloth or reeds
Why: For many days outside or for many people, a pit keeps flies and disease away.
What you need
  • shovel and pickaxe
  • thick boards
  • wooden lid
  • ash or soil
  • cloth or reeds for walls
Step by step
  1. Choose a spot at least 30 m from a well, spring or stream, and lower than them.
  2. Dig a pit 1–1.5 m deep and 60–80 cm wide.
  3. If you hit water while digging, stop and fill it. Find another spot.
  4. Lay strong boards that rest 30 cm past each side.
  5. Leave a 20×30 cm hole and make a lid.
  6. Build a wall of cloth or reeds around it.
  7. After each use, throw in a shovel of ash or soil. Close the lid.
  8. When it is filled to 50 cm from the top, fill it with soil and dig a new one.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Our grandparents always put the outhouse at the edge of the yard, downwind of the house.
⚠ Careful: In soft soil the walls can collapse: do not climb into a deep pit. Always cover the pit — danger for children and animals. Wash hands every time.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.13

Tippy-tap handwashing station

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① jerrycan with a tiny hole in the neck ② forked posts and crossbar ③ rope from the neck ④ foot pedal ⑤ soap on a string ⑥ gravel underneath
Why: You wash hands with little water without touching anything. Handwashing stops most diarrhoea.
What you need
  • 3–5 litre jerrycan with handle
  • 2 forked sticks (1.5 m) and one crossbar
  • rope
  • nail
  • soap
  • gravel
Step by step
  1. Push the two sticks into the ground, 1 m apart.
  2. Lay the crossbar in the forks.
  3. Heat the nail and make a 2–3 mm hole in the neck of the jerrycan.
  4. Hang the jerrycan by its handle from the crossbar.
  5. Tie a rope from the neck down to a pedal stick on the ground.
  6. Tie the soap with string to the crossbar.
  7. Spread gravel underneath, so no mud forms.
  8. Press the pedal: the can tilts and a little water runs. Scrub for 20 seconds.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A bar of soap inside an old sock hanging on a string never gets lost or melts in mud.
⚠ Careful: For handwashing only, not for drinking. Change the water every 1–2 days. Careful with the hot nail — hold it with pliers.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.14

Wood-ash lye (alisiva) for washing

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 evening + overnight
① sift the fine white ash ② boil with water and stir ③ ash settles at the bottom ④ pour the clear liquid through a cloth ⑤ always wear gloves
Why: Without detergent, grandmothers washed with alisiva (wood-ash lye). It removes grease and stains from cotton and linen.
What you need
  • white ash from clean wood
  • sieve
  • metal bucket or pot (not aluminium)
  • wooden stirring stick
  • cloth
  • rubber gloves and goggles
Step by step
  1. Sift the ash. Keep only the fine white part.
  2. Mix 1 part ash with 5 parts water.
  3. Boil for 30 minutes, stirring with the stick.
  4. Leave it overnight to settle.
  5. In the morning, with gloves, pour off the clear liquid through a cloth.
  6. Lye is yellowish and feels slippery on the fingers.
  7. Soak clothes 1–2 hours, then scrub.
  8. Rinse very well, twice, with clean water.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The ash left at the bottom is good for compost or for scouring pots.
⚠ Careful: Lye BURNS (caustic): gloves and goggles. If it gets in an eye, rinse with water for 15 minutes and see a doctor. Never in aluminium. No ash from painted wood, coal or paper. It ruins wool and silk. Keep away from children.
💧 Water & Hygiene · 1.15

Washing clothes by hand

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1–2 hours
① soak in the tub ② bucket washer with plunger ③ wring by twisting ④ hang in the sun with pegs
Why: Without power, clean clothes keep away lice, skin problems and illness.
What you need
  • washtub or large basin
  • 20-litre bucket with lid
  • new sink plunger (for a 'bucket washer')
  • soap
  • rope and clothes pegs
Step by step
  1. Separate whites from colours and very dirty items.
  2. Soak in warm soapy water, 30 minutes or overnight.
  3. Scrub stains with soap, on a board or a stone.
  4. Bucket washer: add clothes and water to half full. Pump the plunger up and down 2–3 minutes.
  5. Rinse twice in clean water.
  6. Wring: twist the item from both ends, in opposite directions.
  7. Hang in the sun. Whites in full sun, colours inside out.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Cut a hole in the bucket lid for the plunger handle. No splashing.
⚠ Careful: Clothes of sick people and nappies: separately, hot water or boiling, and gloves. Protect your back — bend your knees when lifting wet laundry.
Chapter 2

Fire, Heat & Light

Fire was humanity’s first tool. It gives heat, light, boiled water and cooked food. Here you learn to light it without matches, keep it alive, stay warm safely and make your own light.
  1. Building a fire: teepee and log-cabin lays
  2. Finding and preparing tinder
  3. Making char cloth in a tin
  4. Fire with a ferro rod or flint and steel
  5. Bow drill fire
  6. Fire with a magnifying glass or a water bottle
  7. Keeping embers overnight and carrying fire
  8. Rocket stove from bricks
  9. Using a wood stove or fireplace safely
  10. Cutting, splitting and drying firewood
  11. Making charcoal in a closed metal barrel
  12. Olive oil lamp (votive-lamp style)
  13. Making candles from beeswax or tallow
  14. Keeping warm without power: one warm room
  15. Hot stones: bed warmer and cooking
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.1

Building a fire: teepee and log-cabin lays

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes
① tinder ② twigs (kindling) ③ thick wood (fuel) ④ log cabin of crossed logs ⑤ stone ring ⑥ small teepee inside the log cabin
Why: Fire gives heat, boiled water, cooking and light. Built the right way, it lights with one match.
What you need
  • Tinder: dry grass, bark shavings, paper
  • Dry twigs, from match to pencil thickness
  • Wood as thick as your wrist and thicker
  • Stones for a ring
  • Matches or a lighter
Step by step
  1. Pick a spot with no dry grass, 3 metres from trees and tents.
  2. Clear the ground and make a ring of stones.
  3. Gather BEFORE lighting: two handfuls of tinder, an armful of twigs, an armful of wood.
  4. Teepee: put tinder in the middle. Lean twigs around it like a pointed tent.
  5. Leave a small "door" on the windward side to light it.
  6. Log cabin: around the teepee, stack wood in crossed pairs, like a square well.
  7. Light the tinder at the bottom. Blow gently at the base.
  8. Add thick wood only when the thin wood burns well.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The teepee lights fast and boils water. The log cabin burns steadily and leaves good embers for cooking.
⚠ Careful: Many countries ban outdoor fires in summer; obey local rules. Keep water or soil close. Never leave a fire alone. Put it out with water and stirring until the ash is cold to the hand.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.2

Finding and preparing tinder

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① nest of dry grass ② birch bark curl ③ fatwood and shavings ④ feather stick with curls
Why: Every fire starts from tinder: something very dry and fine that catches a spark. Without good tinder, even matches fail.
What you need
  • Knife
  • Dry grass, pine needles
  • Birch or cypress bark
  • Fatwood (resin-soaked pine)
  • Dry stick without bark
  • Bag that closes
Step by step
  1. Collect only what snaps with a "crack". If it bends, it is damp.
  2. Rub dry grass between your palms until it is like wool. Shape a nest.
  3. Scrape birch or cypress bark into thin fibres.
  4. Find fatwood: an old pine stump with yellow resin that smells of turpentine.
  5. Scrape the fatwood into fine shavings.
  6. Feather stick: carve thin curls down a dry stick.
  7. Leave the curls attached, like feathers.
  8. Put the finest in the middle of the nest, coarser outside.
  9. Keep tinder in a closed bag, always dry.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Fatwood lights even when wet, and one piece lasts for years. Cotton wool rubbed with petroleum jelly is also excellent.
⚠ Careful: Always cut with the blade away from your body and legs. Do not strip bark from living trees. Take bark only from fallen branches.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.3

Making char cloth in a tin

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① cotton squares ② small hole in the lid ③ smoke comes out of the hole ④ embers ⑤ finished black char cloth catching a spark
Why: Char cloth (cotton turned to charcoal) catches the tiniest spark. With it you light fire with flint and steel or a lens.
What you need
  • Small metal tin with a lid
  • Nail
  • Old 100% cotton cloth (jeans, T-shirt)
  • Scissors
  • Embers or a fire
  • Tongs or a glove
Step by step
  1. Cut the cloth into 5×5 cm squares.
  2. Make one small hole in the lid with the nail.
  3. Fill the tin loosely with the squares and close it.
  4. Set the tin on the embers, outdoors.
  5. Smoke, maybe a small flame, comes out of the hole. Wait.
  6. When the smoke stops (10–15 minutes), lift the tin out with tongs.
  7. Let it cool CLOSED. Opened hot, the cloth will burn.
  8. Store the black squares in the same tin.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Good char cloth is black and soft. Brown = needs more time. Crumbles = cooked too long.
⚠ Careful: Only cotton or linen. Synthetic cloth melts and gives toxic smoke. Do it outdoors and do not breathe the smoke. The tin gets very hot.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.4

Fire with a ferro rod or flint and steel

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 10 minutes (with practice)
① ferro rod (pulled back) ② striker ③ tinder nest ④ flint stone ⑤ steel striker ⑥ char cloth on the stone
Why: A ferro rod (a metal rod that throws sparks) lights thousands of fires, wet or dry. Matches run out; this lasts for years.
What you need
  • Ferro rod and striker (or the back of a steel knife)
  • Or: hard flint stone and a steel striker
  • Char cloth
  • Nest of dry grass
  • Twigs ready
Step by step
  1. Prepare the nest and twigs BEFORE making sparks.
  2. Ferro rod: rest its tip inside the tinder.
  3. Hold the striker still on the rod, at 45°.
  4. Pull the rod back, firm and slow. This keeps the nest intact.
  5. When it smokes, lift the nest and blow gently until it flames.
  6. Flint and steel: put a bit of char cloth on the stone, near the sharp edge.
  7. Strike the steel downward, scraping the stone’s edge.
  8. When the char cloth glows, put it in the nest and blow.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A new rod has a black coating. Scrape it off first, or it will not spark.
⚠ Careful: Sparks are burning metal, over 1,000 °C. Keep them away from eyes, clothes and dry grass. Never strike toward the hand holding the stone.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.5

Bow drill fire

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: Half a day to make; lots of practice
① bow ② cord, one turn around the spindle ③ spindle ④ top stone ⑤ fireboard ⑥ foot holds the board ⑦ leaf to catch the coal ⑧ pit and notch, seen from above
Why: The oldest way: fire from only wood and cord. It is hard, but needs nothing bought.
What you need
  • Dry soft wood: lime, willow, poplar, cypress
  • Knife
  • Strong cord
  • Slightly curved stick for the bow, as long as your arm
  • Stone with a small dip, for the top
  • Leaf or bark, tinder nest
Step by step
  1. Spindle: straight dry stick, 20 cm long, thumb-thick, pointed at both ends.
  2. Fireboard: a board 2 cm thick. Carve a small pit 1 cm from the edge.
  3. Cut a notch like a slice of pie, from the pit to the edge.
  4. Tie the cord a little loose on the bow. Twist it once around the spindle.
  5. Hold the board with your foot. Put a leaf under the notch.
  6. Press the spindle down with the stone. Brace your wrist on your knee.
  7. Saw the bow back and forth, full length. Slow first, then fast.
  8. When there is thick smoke and black dust, do 20 more strokes.
  9. Put the glowing coal from the notch into the nest and blow gently.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Put a little grease or a leaf under the top stone so the top spins easily. Keep the bottom dry.
⚠ Careful: The wood must be bone-dry. Take care with the knife when carving. Keep your back straight and rest often.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.6

Fire with a magnifying glass or a water bottle

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 5–15 minutes in strong sun
① sun ② lens ③ tiny bright dot ④ char cloth ⑤ bottle full of water
Why: The sun lights fire for free, with no matches. It works only under a clear sky, mostly at midday.
What you need
  • Magnifying glass
  • Or reading glasses (for close-up)
  • Or a round clear bottle full of water
  • Char cloth, black paper or dry rotten wood
  • Tinder nest
Step by step
  1. Work at midday, with high sun and no clouds.
  2. Put the char cloth on a dry spot, sheltered from wind.
  3. Hold the lens square to the sun.
  4. Raise or lower the lens until the light is a tiny bright dot.
  5. Keep your hand still. Rest your elbow on your knee.
  6. Bottle: fill it to the top with no bubbles. Try 3–8 cm distance.
  7. When the char cloth glows and smokes, put it in the nest and blow.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Black catches faster. With no char cloth, blacken paper with charcoal.
⚠ Careful: Do not stare at the sun or the bright dot: it harms the eyes. Glasses for short sight (distance) will not work. Never leave lenses or water bottles in the sun on dry grass: wildfires start this way.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.7

Keeping embers overnight and carrying fire

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 10 minutes in the evening
① heap of coals ② 3–5 cm layer of ash ③ ground ④ tin with small holes ⑤ wire handle ⑥ moss with one live coal
Why: If the embers stay alive until morning, you relight in minutes. You save matches and tinder.
What you need
  • Fire with good embers from hardwood (oak, olive)
  • Ash
  • Small shovel
  • Metal tin with lid and a wire handle
  • Dry moss or tinder fungus
Step by step
  1. In the evening, rake the coals into one heap in the middle.
  2. Lay one thick hardwood log on top.
  3. Cover the whole heap with 3–5 cm of ash. No red should show.
  4. In the morning, uncover, put tinder on the embers and blow.
  5. To carry fire: punch a few small holes low and high in the tin.
  6. Put in dry moss and one live coal on top. Close the lid.
  7. Swing it a little every half hour for air.
  8. If it is dying, open a little. If it flares, plug holes with mud.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: In old villages the hearth fire was kept all winter, covered with ash.
⚠ Careful: Live coals can stay in ash for up to 3 days. Never dump ash in a bag or plastic bin. The tin gets hot: hold it by the wire. Covered embers indoors without a chimney make carbon monoxide.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.8

Rocket stove from bricks

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour
① sticks go in through the door ② air enters under the grate ③ brick chimney ④ pot on stones, with a gap ⑤ strong flame
Why: A rocket stove burns hot and clean on a few twigs. It needs much less wood than an open fire.
What you need
  • 16–20 bricks
  • Grate or metal bar for a shelf
  • Dry sticks, finger-thick
  • Three small stones
  • Cooking pot
Step by step
  1. On flat bare ground, lay bricks in a U shape. The open end is the door.
  2. Make the door about 10×10 cm.
  3. Put a grate inside at half height. Sticks go on top, air goes under.
  4. Over the back part, build a chimney 40–50 cm high, with no gaps.
  5. Put three stones on top. Leave a 2 cm gap under the pot.
  6. Light some paper inside, then push sticks in through the door.
  7. Add a few sticks often. Push them in as they burn.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: It can also be made from cans: an L-shaped tube inside a big can, with ash around it as insulation.
⚠ Careful: Outdoors only, never indoors. Bricks stay hot for hours. No river stones or concrete blocks: they can crack and burst. Obey summer fire bans.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.9

Using a wood stove or fireplace safely

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: Daily; cleaning once a year
① stove ② chimney pipe (sweep yearly) ③ window slightly open ④ CO alarm on the ceiling ⑤ chimney brush ⑥ metal floor plate and 1 m clear space
Why: A wood stove or fireplace heats and cooks without power. But indoors, one mistake can kill.
What you need
  • Stove or fireplace with a drawing chimney
  • Battery carbon monoxide (CO) alarm
  • Fire extinguisher or bucket of sand
  • Metal plate on the floor
  • Chimney brush
  • Dry firewood
Step by step
  1. Burn only dry wood. Never plastic or painted wood.
  2. Open the chimney damper before lighting.
  3. Leave a window open 2 cm for fresh air.
  4. Keep furniture, clothes and wood 1 metre from the stove.
  5. Put a CO alarm in the room and in the bedroom.
  6. Do not shut the air fully at night to make it last. That makes carbon monoxide.
  7. Sweep the chimney with the brush once a year, before winter.
  8. Take ash out in a metal bucket with a lid, outside the house.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: If smoke comes back in, hold burning paper high up at the chimney opening to warm it so it draws.
⚠ Careful: Carbon monoxide has no smell and cannot be seen. Headache, dizziness, sleepiness or vomiting: everyone out at once, call emergency (112 in Europe). Never use a charcoal brazier, barbecue or generator indoors.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.10

Cutting, splitting and drying firewood

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: A few hours’ work + 1 year drying
① chopping block ② axe ③ cracks: strike here ④ stack raised on beams ⑤ cover on top only ⑥ air passes through
Why: Green wood smokes, gives little heat and dirties the chimney. Dry wood burns clean and gives almost twice the heat.
What you need
  • Saw
  • Splitting axe, or sledgehammer and wedge
  • Thick chopping block
  • Gloves, goggles, strong boots
  • Pallets or two beams
  • Metal sheet or tarp for a cover
Step by step
  1. Saw logs into 30–40 cm rounds, to fit your stove.
  2. Stand each round upright on the chopping block.
  3. Strike along the cracks in the end, not on knots.
  4. Split into pieces from wrist to forearm thick.
  5. Stack on pallets, 10–15 cm above the ground.
  6. Leave gaps so air can pass.
  7. Cover only the top. Leave the sides open to sun and wind.
  8. Dry 1 year (oak 2). It is ready when the ends crack.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Cut this year, burn next year. Two dry pieces knocked together ring "clack"; green ones go "thud".
⚠ Careful: Wear goggles and strong boots. Stand with feet apart, so a glancing axe hits the ground. Nobody near you while chopping. Do not cut trees in forests without a permit.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.11

Making charcoal in a closed metal barrel

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 4–6 hours + 1 day cooling
① closed barrel ② wood packed tight ③ small hole in the lid ④ gas burning ⑤ fire underneath ⑥ bricks ⑦ finished charcoal
Why: Charcoal burns hot, with no flame and little smoke. It is light, keeps for years, and suits cooking and metalwork.
What you need
  • Clean metal barrel with a lid
  • Dry hardwood pieces, 10–20 cm
  • Bricks for a stand
  • Plenty of wood for the fire underneath
  • Mud
  • Thick gloves, shovel, water
Step by step
  1. Make 1–2 holes of 1 cm in the lid.
  2. Pack the barrel tight with wood. Close the lid well.
  3. Set the barrel on bricks, 25 cm above the ground.
  4. Light a strong fire under and around it.
  5. In 1–2 hours white smoke comes out. Then the gas at the holes catches fire.
  6. Keep the fire going until the little flames at the holes die out.
  7. Seal the holes with mud. Let the fire die.
  8. Do not open until fully cold (12–24 hours), or it bursts into flame.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Good charcoal is black, shiny, light, and rings like glass when tapped.
⚠ Careful: Outdoors only, far from houses and dry grass, never on fire-ban days. Smoke and gas are toxic. Never use a barrel that held fuel or chemicals: it can explode. Burn charcoal only in the open air.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.12

Olive oil lamp (votive-lamp style)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes
① jar ② water ③ 1–2 cm of oil ④ cork slice ⑤ wick ⑥ foil on top of the cork
Why: A floating-wick oil lamp gives a small, steady light all night on a little oil. Our grandmothers lit one every evening.
What you need
  • Glass jar or tumbler
  • Water
  • Olive oil or other vegetable oil
  • Bottle cork
  • Aluminium foil
  • Cotton wick or cotton string
Step by step
  1. Fill the jar two-thirds with water.
  2. Pour 1–2 cm of oil on top. The oil floats.
  3. Cut a 5 mm slice of cork.
  4. Cover the top of the slice with foil so it will not burn.
  5. Pierce the middle with a nail and thread the wick through.
  6. Leave 3–5 mm of wick above and 1–2 cm below, in the oil.
  7. Float the cork. Wait 5 minutes for the wick to soak.
  8. Light it. If it smokes, trim the wick shorter.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The water below keeps the jar cool and puts the flame out when the oil runs out.
⚠ Careful: Set it on a steady surface, away from curtains, children and cats. Never use petrol, alcohol or kerosene: they flare up. Do not leave it burning when you go out.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.13

Making candles from beeswax or tallow

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2–3 hours
① pot of water (double boiler) ② tin of melted wax ③ wicks tied to a stick ④ dip and lift, again and again ⑤ mould ⑥ pencil holds the wick centred
Why: Candles give light without power and keep for years. Make them from beeswax or tallow (melted animal fat).
What you need
  • Beeswax or beef/mutton tallow
  • Pot of water
  • Tall tin can
  • Cotton wick or thick cotton string
  • Stick and pencil
  • Mould: paper milk carton
  • Small nut as a weight
Step by step
  1. Melt the wax in the tin, standing in a pot of simmering water.
  2. Tallow: melt it, strain through cloth, and melt again to clean it.
  3. Dipped: tie a 25 cm wick to a stick, with a nut on the end.
  4. Dip for 2–3 seconds, lift, and let it cool 1 minute.
  5. Repeat 20–30 times until thick. Then cut off the nut.
  6. Mould: hang the wick in the centre, tied to a pencil.
  7. Pour the wax slowly. Leave 12 hours, then tear off the mould.
  8. Trim the wick to 5 mm before lighting.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A little beeswax mixed into tallow makes a harder candle with less smell.
⚠ Careful: Never heat wax directly over the flame: it ignites. If it catches fire, cover it with a lid. NEVER put water on burning wax or fat. Never leave a lit candle unattended.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.14

Keeping warm without power: one warm room

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour to set up
① heavy curtains closed ② towel under the door ③ rug ④ hat and layers ⑤ hot water bottle
Why: Without power you cannot heat the whole house. Heat one small room and all stay there together.
What you need
  • The smallest sunny room
  • Blankets, heavy curtains
  • Towels for gaps
  • Rugs
  • Woollens: hat, socks, jumpers
  • Hot water bottle
Step by step
  1. Choose one small room, ideally south-facing. Close the others.
  2. Hang blankets over doors to the other rooms.
  3. By day open curtains where sun comes in. At night close shutters and curtains.
  4. Put a rolled towel under the door and in gaps.
  5. Lay rugs or blankets on the floor.
  6. Dress like an onion: many thin layers, a hat, wool socks.
  7. Fill the hot water bottle with hot, not boiling, water. Use it on your body or in bed.
  8. Sleep close together under many blankets.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Eat hot food and drink warm drinks. The body makes heat from food.
⚠ Careful: Never use a charcoal brazier, camping gas or barbecue indoors for heat: carbon monoxide kills in sleep. If you burn anything, keep some ventilation. Wrap the hot water bottle in a towel. Babies and the elderly chill faster: watch them.
🔥 Fire, Heat & Light · 2.15

Hot stones: bed warmer and cooking

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour
① dry stone at the edge of the fire ② wrapped stone at the foot of the bed ③ tongs drop a hot stone into water ④ steam: the water heats ⑤ river stone: NO!
Why: A hot stone holds heat for hours. It warms a bed and can boil water in a container that cannot go on the fire.
What you need
  • Dry field stones, potato-sized
  • A fire
  • Tongs or two sticks
  • Old towel or wool cloth
  • Wooden bowl or bucket for cooking
Step by step
  1. Pick dry, solid stones with no cracks. NOT from rivers or the sea.
  2. Set the stones at the edge of the fire for 30–60 minutes.
  3. Bed warmer: lift a stone with tongs and let it cool a little.
  4. Wrap it in 2–3 layers of cloth. Put it at the foot of the bed before sleep.
  5. Cooking: shake off the ash and drop the stone into the water.
  6. Take out cool stones, add new hot ones. After a few changes the water boils.
  7. On a flat hot stone you can also bake flatbread or thin meat.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A brick does the same job. Grandmother warmed a brick by the hearth and wrapped it in flannel.
⚠ Careful: River and sea stones hold water inside. In a fire they can burst and throw sharp pieces. Never put a hot stone in bed without cloth. Not for babies or anyone with poor feeling in the feet (e.g. diabetes).
Chapter 3

Keeping food without a fridge

Dedicated to Grandma Maria ♥ and to the memory of Grandma Areti ✝
Before the fridge, every home had a cellar, crocks and jars. With salt, sun, smoke, vinegar, sugar and fat, our grandparents kept summer food for the whole winter. Here you will learn these simple ways — and how to stay safe.
  1. Salting fish: sardines and anchovies in salt
  2. Dry-salting and air-drying meat
  3. Sun-drying fruit and vegetables
  4. Building a simple solar food dryer
  5. Smoking fish and meat in a barrel
  6. Pickles in vinegar (toursi)
  7. Sauerkraut: fermented cabbage with salt only
  8. Curing olives at home
  9. Kavourmas: meat preserved in its own fat
  10. Jars in a boiling water bath (acidic foods only)
  11. Storing potatoes, onions, carrots and apples
  12. Pot-in-pot clay cooler (zeer)
  13. Keeping eggs for months
  14. Preserving fruit with sugar and grape must
  15. Protecting stored food from mice, insects and damp
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.1

Salting fish: sardines and anchovies in salt

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour of work + 1–3 months of waiting
① pinch off the head here ② clean fish, head off ③ layer of fish ④ layer of coarse salt ⑤ plate and stone as weight ⑥ brine covers everything
Why: Salt pulls the water out of the fish, so germs cannot live. It keeps for months without a fridge.
What you need
  • Very fresh small fish (sardines, anchovies)
  • Coarse salt (about 1 kg for every 2 kg of fish)
  • Clay or glass container
  • Plate and a clean stone as a weight
Step by step
  1. Pinch off the head with your fingers and pull the guts out with it.
  2. Do not wash in fresh water. If needed, rinse in sea water or salty water.
  3. Spread a 1 cm layer of salt on the bottom of the container.
  4. Lay one row of fish, belly to belly, and cover them fully with salt.
  5. Repeat the layers to the top. Finish with a thick layer of salt.
  6. Put a plate and a stone on top. In 1–2 days brine (salty liquid) appears.
  7. The brine must always cover the fish. If low, add brine of 1 cup salt to 3 cups water.
  8. Keep in a cool, dark place. Sardines are ready in 1 month, anchovies in 2–3.
  9. Before eating, rinse, soak 30 minutes in water and remove the bone. Add olive oil.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Old fishermen said: "Fish must not see fresh water." Salt it the same evening it is caught.
⚠ Careful: Only very fresh fish — stale fish can poison you even when salted. If it smells rotten, feels slimy or swells, throw it away. Very salty: careful with high blood pressure.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.2

Dry-salting and air-drying meat

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 1 hour + 3–6 weeks
① 30 g salt per kg, rubbed in all over ② tray in a cold place, turned daily ③ roofed, shady, airy place ④ thermometer: 10–15°C ⑤ air flow to dry it
Why: In the old days, meat from the winter pig was salted and lasted all year. Salt, cold and air do the work.
What you need
  • Whole piece of boneless meat (e.g. pork loin or neck)
  • Salt: 30 grams for every kg of meat
  • Kitchen scale
  • Pepper, savory, garlic (if you have them)
  • Cheesecloth or net, string
Step by step
  1. Do it only in winter, when it is below 10°C outside.
  2. Weigh the meat. Weigh 30 g of salt for every kg, plus the spices.
  3. Rub the salt well all over the piece, also into the folds.
  4. Put it in a closed container in a cold place (below 5°C).
  5. Leave 1 day for every centimetre of thickness. Turn it every day.
  6. Rinse quickly, dry it and wrap it in cheesecloth or net.
  7. Hang it in a shady, airy place, 10–15°C, away from flies.
  8. Weigh again. It is ready when it has lost 1/3 of its weight (3–6 weeks).
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: A little white powdery mould outside is normal; wipe it with a cloth dipped in vinegar.
⚠ Careful: Whole pieces only — never minced meat or sausage without experience. Weigh the salt exactly. Green, black or fuzzy mould, slime or a rotten smell: throw it away. Raw cured meat is not for pregnant women, small children or the sick.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.3

Sun-drying fruit and vegetables

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 3–7 sunny days
① the sun ② tulle against flies ③ halved apricots, cut side up ④ halved tomatoes with a little salt ⑤ mesh tray raised on trestles ⑥ air passes underneath
Why: The sun is free energy. Dried figs, raisins, apricots and tomatoes last all winter.
What you need
  • Ripe, sound fruit or tomatoes
  • Trays with mesh, or reed mats
  • Fine net (tulle) against flies
  • Knife, a little salt
  • Glass jars
Step by step
  1. Wash and dry the fruit. Throw away any that are bruised or rotten.
  2. Cut apricots and tomatoes in half. Remove the stones.
  3. Sprinkle tomatoes with a little salt. Figs stay whole or opened in two.
  4. Lay them on the mesh, cut side up, not touching each other.
  5. Raise the tray on trestles so air passes underneath.
  6. Cover with tulle and hold it down with stones.
  7. Turn them every day. In the evening bring them inside, away from the dew.
  8. They are ready when leathery and no juice comes out when squeezed.
  9. Put them in jars. Shake daily for 1 week. If you see moisture, dry them again.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Grandmothers dipped figs for a few seconds in boiling sea water; they dry faster and get fewer worms.
⚠ Careful: Never put them on the bare ground. Throw away any that go mouldy. Dried tomatoes in oil without vinegar and a fridge can cause botulism (deadly food poisoning) — keep them dry.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.4

Building a simple solar food dryer

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 days to build
① air inlet with mesh ② glass or clear plastic ③ black bottom that heats up ④ mesh trays with fruit ⑤ air outlet with mesh and cap ⑥ warm air rises through the trays
Why: It dries food faster than open sun, with no flies, dust or dew. It works even on slightly humid days.
What you need
  • Wood and plywood
  • Glass or thick clear plastic sheet
  • Black paint or black metal sheet
  • Insect mesh (for 3–4 trays and the air holes)
  • Nails, screws, hinges
Step by step
  1. Build a long, shallow box, about 2 m × 1 m (the collector).
  2. Paint the bottom black or lay black metal sheet. Cover with glass or plastic.
  3. Leave the lower end open and close it with mesh: air comes in there.
  4. Build a tall cabinet with a back door. Fit 3–4 mesh trays inside.
  5. Join the top end of the collector to the bottom of the cabinet.
  6. Make an air hole at the top of the cabinet, with mesh and a rain cap.
  7. Face the collector south, tilted about 30°.
  8. Put in a thermometer. You want 45–60°C. If hotter, open the top hole more.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Cut fruit into slices 0.5–1 cm thick. Thin slices dry in 1–3 days.
⚠ Careful: Do not use painted or chemically treated wood, or galvanised mesh touching food. Glass can break — fix it in a frame and wear gloves.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.5

Smoking fish and meat in a barrel

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 1 day to build; 3–8 hours of smoking
① hot smoking: fire under the drum ② grill with fish ③ cold smoking: fire pit ④ buried pipe — the smoke cools ⑤ drum higher up with hanging fish ⑥ lid slightly open for draught
Why: Smoke dries the surface and keeps insects and germs away. Smoked fish keeps longer than fresh fish.
What you need
  • Clean metal drum (bottom removed or with holes)
  • Grill or rods and hooks
  • Dry hardwood: oak, beech, olive, fruit trees
  • Salt (80 g in 1 litre of water)
  • Thermometer
Step by step
  1. First burn the empty drum with a fire to burn off any paint and dirt.
  2. Put fish in brine of 80 g salt per litre for 1 hour (meat 4–8 hours).
  3. Hang it in the air for 1–2 hours until the surface feels a little sticky.
  4. Hot smoking: fire under the drum, 70–90°C, for 3–6 hours.
  5. Fish is ready when it comes off the bone. Meat must be fully cooked inside.
  6. Cold smoking: fire in a pit 2–3 m away, smoke travels through a buried pipe.
  7. In cold smoking the smoke stays below 30°C. It does not cook — salt well first.
  8. Keep the wood smouldering: you want thin white smoke, not flames or black smoke.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: A wet sack over the drum holds the smoke in and controls the draught.
⚠ Careful: Never indoors: smoke contains carbon monoxide, which kills without a smell. Never a drum that held fuel or chemicals. Never pine, plywood or painted wood. Cold-smoked food is not cooked.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.6

Pickles in vinegar (toursi)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1–2 hours + 2–4 weeks
① vinegar: 1 part ② water: at most 1 part (same level) ③ salt: 1 tablespoon per litre ④ vegetables packed tightly ⑤ 1 cm space under the lid ⑥ hot brine covering everything
Why: Vinegar is sour and dangerous germs cannot live in it. Summer vegetables become winter food.
What you need
  • Fresh vegetables: peppers, carrots, cauliflower, small cucumbers, celery
  • Strong wine vinegar (5–6%)
  • Water, salt
  • Garlic, dill, peppercorns
  • Clean glass jars with lids
Step by step
  1. Wash the jars and warm them in hot water.
  2. Wash the vegetables and cut them into pieces.
  3. Make the brine: 1 part vinegar and no more than 1 part water.
  4. Add 1 tablespoon of salt for each litre of brine. Bring it to the boil.
  5. Pack the jars tightly with vegetables, garlic, dill and pepper.
  6. Pour the hot brine to cover them. Leave 1 cm of space under the lid.
  7. Close well. To keep for months, boil the jars 10 minutes (see "Jars in boiling water").
  8. Store in a cool, dark place. Ready to eat in 2–4 weeks.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: A vine or sour-cherry leaf in the jar keeps pickles crunchy.
⚠ Careful: Never more water than vinegar — it loses its protection. Vegetables must always be covered. Cloudy with foam, slimy, bad-smelling, or a bulging lid: throw it away without tasting.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.7

Sauerkraut: fermented cabbage with salt only

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour + 1–4 weeks
① sliced cabbage with 20 g salt per kg ② squeeze and press until juice comes out ③ cabbage packed tightly ④ juice covers the cabbage ⑤ weight: small jar of water ⑥ cloth tied on top
Why: No vinegar and no fire: good bacteria sour the cabbage and protect it. It gives vitamin C all winter.
What you need
  • Cabbage
  • Non-iodised salt: 20 g for every kg of cabbage (2%)
  • Scale
  • Large glass jar or clay crock
  • Weight: small jar of water or a clean stone
  • Cloth and a rubber band or string
Step by step
  1. Remove the outer leaves and keep 1–2 clean ones. Slice the cabbage thinly.
  2. Weigh the cabbage. Weigh 20 g of salt for every kg.
  3. Mix and squeeze with your hands for 5–10 minutes until juice comes out.
  4. Press it into the jar a little at a time with your fist, leaving no air.
  5. The juice must cover the cabbage. Put a whole leaf on top.
  6. Put the weight on to keep it under the juice. Cover with a cloth.
  7. Leave it in a room at 18–22°C. In the first days press it down daily.
  8. Taste after 1 week. When it is sour enough for you, move it somewhere cool.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: If there is not enough juice, add brine: 20 g of salt in 1 litre of water.
⚠ Careful: Anything above the juice goes mouldy. A thin white film on top: skim it off. Pink, black or fuzzy mould, slime or a rotten smell: throw away the whole jar. Leave space, as it foams and can overflow.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.8

Curing olives at home

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour + 3–6 weeks
① slits in the green olive ② change the water every day ③ the egg floats: the brine is right ④ layer of olive oil on top
Why: Olives are a nourishing, oily food that keeps a year. Raw they are very bitter; water and salt take the bitterness out.
What you need
  • Sound olives without bruises
  • Knife or stone for cracking
  • Glass jars or a food-safe bucket
  • Salt, water, one fresh egg
  • Lemon, oregano, vinegar, olive oil
Step by step
  1. Green olives: slit each olive 2–3 times or crack it lightly with a stone.
  2. Cover them with water. Change the water every day for 10–20 days.
  3. Taste one. When there is little bitterness and you like it, stop.
  4. Make brine: add salt to water until a fresh egg floats, showing a coin-sized patch.
  5. Put the olives in jars with the brine, a little vinegar, lemon and oregano.
  6. Pour a finger of olive oil on top. Close and wait 2–3 weeks.
  7. Salt-cured black olives: put ripe black olives in a basket with coarse salt.
  8. Toss them every day. The bitter juice drips out. Ready in 3–5 weeks.
  9. Shake off the salt and mix them with a little olive oil and oregano.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: The egg is the old "scale" for brine. If it sinks, add more salt.
⚠ Careful: Olives must always be covered by brine. Soft, slimy or bad-smelling: throw them away. Do not use lye (caustic soda) without an experienced person — it burns skin and eyes. Very salty: careful with high blood pressure.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.9

Kavourmas: meat preserved in its own fat

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 day
① meat simmers in fat over a low fire ② clean clay pot ③ pieces of cooked meat ④ fat at least 2 cm above the meat ⑤ cloth or lid
Why: Well-cooked meat sealed under fat sees no air and lasts the winter. This is how the winter pig was saved.
What you need
  • Pork (or lamb, goat) cut in cubes
  • Pork fat (lard) to melt
  • Salt: 20–30 g per kg, pepper
  • Deep pot
  • Clean clay or glass containers
Step by step
  1. Salt the meat (20–30 g per kg) and leave it overnight somewhere cold.
  2. Melt the fat in the pot over low heat.
  3. Add the meat so the fat covers it. Simmer for 2–3 hours, stirring.
  4. It is ready when soft and fully cooked inside, with no pink.
  5. Warm the clean containers. Put the meat in while hot.
  6. Pour hot fat to cover the meat by at least 2 cm.
  7. Let it set. Cover with a cloth or lid.
  8. Store in a cold, dark place (below 10°C). Eat it within 2–3 months.
  9. Take some with a clean spoon. Re-cover with fat. Heat well before eating.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The fat from kavourmas is also cooking fat; nothing is wasted.
⚠ Careful: No air gets under the fat, and botulism (deadly food poisoning) can grow there. Cook well, store cold, reheat until bubbling hot. Sour or rotten smell: throw it away. Hot fat burns — never add water to it.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.10

Jars in a boiling water bath (acidic foods only)

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2–3 hours
① rack or towel under the jars ② water 3 cm above the lids ③ 1–2 cm of space in the jar ④ strong boil — start timing then ⑤ press the lid: sealed well if it does not "click"
Why: Boiling kills germs and seals the jar airtight. Tomato sauce, fruit and jams keep for over a year.
What you need
  • Glass jars without cracks
  • New lids
  • Big deep pot
  • Rack or folded towel for the bottom
  • Lemon juice (for tomatoes)
  • Tongs or a cloth
Step by step
  1. Wash the jars and keep them warm in hot water.
  2. For tomatoes, add 2 tablespoons of lemon juice to each 1-litre jar.
  3. Fill with the hot food. Leave 1–2 cm of space at the top.
  4. Wipe the rim of the jar. Screw on the lid, not too tight.
  5. Stand the jars on the rack. Water must cover them 3 cm above the lids.
  6. Start timing at a strong boil: jam 10 minutes, fruit 25–30, 1-litre tomato jars 45.
  7. Above 300 metres altitude, add 5 minutes.
  8. Lift the jars out and leave them untouched for 12–24 hours.
  9. Press the centre of the lid. If it does not "click", it sealed well.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Write the date on every jar and eat the oldest first.
⚠ Careful: BOTULISM (deadly poisoning): ONLY for acidic foods. Beans, vegetables, meat, fish and mushrooms need a pressure canner — never a plain boiling water bath. Bulging lid, foam, spurting or bad smell: throw it away without tasting.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.11

Storing potatoes, onions, carrots and apples

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon
① carrots in layers of damp sand ② apples wrapped one by one in paper ③ straw bed at the base ④ heap of potatoes ⑤ 20 cm of straw ⑥ 20 cm of soil ⑦ straw tuft for air ⑧ ditch for rainwater
Why: Many root crops stay alive for months if they have coolness, darkness and the right damp. No power, no jars.
What you need
  • Wooden crates or boxes
  • Damp sand or sawdust
  • Newspaper or paper
  • Straw
  • Shovel (for the clamp)
Step by step
  1. Harvest in dry weather. Do not wash. Keep only sound ones without bruises.
  2. Potatoes: in a dark, cool place, 4–8°C, in airy crates.
  3. Onions and garlic: dry them 2 weeks, braid them, hang them somewhere dry.
  4. Carrots, beetroot: cut the leaves 1 cm above. Bury them in layers of damp sand in a box.
  5. Apples: wrap each one in paper. Store in one layer, away from potatoes.
  6. Garden clamp: lay straw on a dry spot and heap the potatoes on it.
  7. Cover with 20 cm of straw, then 20 cm of soil. Leave a tuft of straw at the top for air.
  8. Dig a ditch around it for rainwater.
  9. Check every month and remove anything rotting before it spoils the rest.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: "One rotten apple spoils the basket" — that is why they checked every month.
⚠ Careful: Green potatoes contain a poison (solanine): cut deep around green parts and sprouts; if very green or bitter, throw them away. Do not store potatoes with onions or apples — they spoil faster.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.12

Pot-in-pot clay cooler (zeer)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① large clay pot ② small pot inside ③ wet sand, 2–3 cm ④ wet cloth as a lid ⑤ water evaporates and takes the heat away ⑥ pour water into the sand
Why: Evaporating water carries heat away, just as a clay jug keeps water cool. Vegetables last days instead of hours.
What you need
  • 2 unglazed clay pots (one fits inside the other)
  • Sand
  • Water
  • Thick cotton cloth or sacking
  • A little clay or a cork for the hole
Step by step
  1. Plug the hole in the bottom of the pots with clay or a cork.
  2. Pour 3 cm of sand into the bottom of the big pot.
  3. Put the small pot inside, leaving a 2–3 cm gap all round.
  4. Fill the gap with sand to the top.
  5. Pour water into the sand until it is well soaked.
  6. Put vegetables and fruit in the inner pot.
  7. Cover with a wet cloth.
  8. Place it in the shade where there is a breeze. Add water 1–2 times a day.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: It works best when the air is hot and dry. In humid weather it cools only a little.
⚠ Careful: It is not a fridge: it cools, but it does not keep meat, fish, milk or cooked food safe for many hours. Wash the cloth often so it does not go mouldy.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.13

Keeping eggs for months

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① lime water (30 g in 1 litre) ② 5 cm of water above the eggs ③ pointed end down ④ sinks and lies flat: fresh — stands up: use soon ⑤ floats: throw it away
Why: Hens lay many eggs in spring and few in winter. Lime water keeps spring eggs until Christmas.
What you need
  • Fresh, unwashed, clean eggs without cracks
  • Slaked (hydrated) lime powder: 30 g per 1 litre of water
  • Large glass jar with a lid
  • Gloves, glasses
  • Bowl of water for testing
Step by step
  1. Do not wash the eggs: they have a natural protective coating. Wipe them only with a dry cloth.
  2. Wearing gloves, mix 30 g of lime into 1 litre of water.
  3. Place the eggs gently in the jar, pointed end down.
  4. Pour in the lime water to cover them by 5 cm.
  5. Close and keep in a cool, dark place. They keep for 8–12 months.
  6. Without lime: rub each fresh egg with a little oil. Keep them in a tray, pointed end down, somewhere cool, for 3–6 months.
  7. Before use, rinse the egg. Put it in water: if it sinks it is good, if it floats throw it away.
  8. Crack each egg into a cup first, to smell it.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: For boiled eggs, prick the wide end with a pin first, or it will crack while boiling.
⚠ Careful: Lime burns skin and eyes: wear gloves and glasses, keep away from children. Only clean, unwashed, sound eggs. Smell every egg. Cook eggs well.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.14

Preserving fruit with sugar and grape must

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 2–4 hours
① fruit and sugar boil over medium heat ② drop on a cold plate: wrinkles = ready ③ hot filled jars ④ petimezi, thick like honey
Why: Lots of sugar, like salt, stops germs living. Petimezi (grape syrup) sweetens with no sugar at all, only grapes.
What you need
  • Ripe fruit (apricots, figs, quinces, bitter oranges, sour cherries)
  • Sugar
  • Lemon
  • Fresh grape must (for petimezi)
  • Stainless pot, wooden spoon, small plate
  • Clean jars
Step by step
  1. Jam: cut the fruit. Weigh it; add 700 g to 1 kg of sugar for each kg of fruit.
  2. Boil over medium heat, stirring, and skim off the foam.
  3. Add the juice of one lemon at the end.
  4. Test: drop some on a cold plate. If it wrinkles when pushed, it is ready.
  5. Spoon sweet: fruit and sugar in equal weights; boil until the syrup thickens.
  6. Fill hot jars, close and boil them 10 minutes in water.
  7. Petimezi: let the must settle overnight. Take the clear part from the top.
  8. Boil it slowly, skimming, until only 1/4 is left. It should be thick like honey.
  9. Pour it hot into clean bottles and close.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: The old ladies added a sprig of rose geranium or an almond to the spoon sweet for scent.
⚠ Careful: Hot syrup sticks to skin and burns badly — keep children away. If mould grows on top, do not just scrape it off; throw away the whole jar. With less sugar it will not keep.
🫙 Keeping food without a fridge · 3.15

Protecting stored food from mice, insects and damp

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon + a monthly check
① closed jars of beans and flour ② bay leaf ③ label with the date ④ shelf 30 cm above the floor ⑤ new at the back, old at the front ⑥ metal bin with a lid ⑦ the mouse cannot reach it
Why: One mouse nest or weevils in the flour can ruin a whole winter of food. A good store is half of survival.
What you need
  • Glass jars with seals, metal tins or bins with lids
  • Bay leaves
  • Labels and a pencil for dates
  • Shelves raised off the floor
  • Small bags of rice or dry salt against damp
Step by step
  1. Put flour, beans, rice and pasta in closed jars or metal tins. Not in paper or plastic bags.
  2. Before closing, kill insect eggs: oven at 60°C for 30 minutes or freezer for 3 days.
  3. Put 2–3 bay leaves in every jar of beans or flour.
  4. Write the date on every jar.
  5. Shelves should be 30 cm above the floor and a little away from the wall.
  6. Block every hole bigger than a pencil. A mouse can get through.
  7. Put new food at the back and old food at the front. Eat the old first.
  8. Keep the store dry and cool, with some air. Add a small bag of rice for damp.
  9. Every month check for insects, mould and droppings.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: One cat in the house is worth ten mousetraps.
⚠ Careful: Mouldy grain, corn or peanuts contain poisons — throw them away, do not even feed them to animals. Never put insect spray on food. Rat poison also kills children, dogs and cats. Wash your hands after touching mouse droppings.
Chapter 4

Bread & the old-time kitchen

Dedicated to Grandma Maria ♥ and to the memory of Grandma Areti ✝
Our grandmothers made bread, cheese, butter and winter food with their own hands. Here you learn to bake, grind and store food without shops or power, and to cook with very little fuel.
  1. Sourdough starter (prozymi) from flour and water — and keeping it alive
  2. Sourdough bread — kneading, rising, baking
  3. Flatbread without yeast on a pan or hot stone
  4. Baking in a cast-iron pot in the embers
  5. Building a simple clay (mud) oven outside
  6. Grinding grain by hand (hand mill) and sifting flour
  7. Paximadi — twice-baked rusks that last a year
  8. Trahanas (sour and sweet) — food that keeps all winter
  9. Homemade pasta — hilopites (egg noodles) and drying
  10. Yogurt at home without a machine
  11. Simple fresh cheese with lemon or vinegar — and using the whey
  12. Butter from cream in a jar — and clarified butter that keeps
  13. Hay-box (retained-heat cooker) — cooking with almost no fuel
  14. Solar oven from a box, foil and glass
  15. Dried beans, lentils, chickpeas: soaking, low-fuel cooking, sprouting — and homemade vinegar
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.1

Sourdough starter (prozymi) from flour and water — and keeping it alive

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 5–7 days (a few minutes a day)
Left day 1, middle day 3, right day 5–7. ① Flour + water 1:1 ② Cloth tied over the mouth ③ Bubbles ④ Rubber band at the level after feeding ⑤ The mix has doubled — ready.
Why: With no shop yeast, a starter makes bread rise. You make it from flour and water only, and it can live for years.
What you need
  • Flour, best wholemeal or rye
  • Water without chlorine (rain, spring, or boiled and cooled)
  • Glass jar and wooden spoon
  • Clean cloth and a rubber band or string
Step by step
  1. Day 1: Mix 50 g flour with 50 ml lukewarm water into a thick paste.
  2. Cover the jar with a cloth and tie it. Keep it warm (20–26 °C).
  3. Every day throw away half and feed it 50 g flour and 50 ml water.
  4. Day 3–4: you will see bubbles and smell something sour. This is good.
  5. After feeding, put a rubber band at the level of the mix as a mark.
  6. Day 5–7: when it doubles in 4–8 hours, the starter is ready.
  7. To keep it: store it in a cool place and feed it once a week.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Grandmothers kept a piece of dough from each baking, with a little salt, for next time. If it is slow to wake, add a spoon of honey or a little grape juice.
⚠ Careful: If you see pink, orange or red streaks, or fuzzy mould, throw away the WHOLE jar and start again. A grey liquid on top only means hunger: stir it in and feed.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.2

Sourdough bread — kneading, rising, baking

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 day (mostly waiting)
① Kneading: push and fold ② The dough rises in the bowl under a cloth ③ It doubles ④ Cuts on the top ⑤ Tray in a very hot oven.
Why: Bread is the base of every meal. With starter, flour, water and salt you bake daily bread without any shop.
What you need
  • 500 g flour
  • 330 ml lukewarm water
  • 100 g active (bubbly) starter
  • 10 g salt (2 teaspoons)
  • Bowl, cloth, tray, oven or cast-iron pot
Step by step
  1. Mix the starter into the water. Add the flour and the salt.
  2. Knead for 10 minutes: push with your palm, fold, turn. Again and again.
  3. The dough is ready when it is smooth and springs back when pressed.
  4. Put it in a bowl, cover with a cloth. Leave 4–8 hours to double.
  5. Shape a round loaf without pressing hard. Leave it another 1–2 hours.
  6. Cut the top with a sharp knife, 1 cm deep.
  7. Bake in a very hot oven (230 °C) for 40–45 minutes.
  8. Tap the bottom: if it sounds hollow, it is done. Let it cool 1 hour.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Put a small tray of water in the oven for the first 15 minutes: the crust comes out crisp. Keep a piece of dough as starter for next time.
⚠ Careful: The oven and tray are very hot: use thick gloves or a folded cloth. Watch out for hot steam when you open the door.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.3

Flatbread without yeast on a pan or hot stone

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 45 minutes
① Ball of dough ② Rolling pin ③ Thin sheet 2–3 mm ④ Pan with the flatbread ⑤ Stones holding the pan ⑥ Small fire underneath.
Why: When you have no oven and no starter, flatbread cooks in minutes on a pan, metal sheet or stone over a fire.
What you need
  • 250 g flour
  • 150 ml lukewarm water
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • 1 tablespoon oil
  • Rolling pin or bottle, pan or flat stone
Step by step
  1. Mix flour, salt, oil and water. Knead for 5 minutes.
  2. Cover the dough with a cloth. Let it rest 30 minutes.
  3. Cut it into 6 small balls.
  4. Roll each ball into a thin sheet, 2–3 mm.
  5. Heat the pan or stone well, with no oil.
  6. Cook each flatbread 1–2 minutes per side, until it puffs and gets brown spots.
  7. Wrap the cooked breads in a cloth to keep them soft.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: A wine bottle works as a rolling pin. If you have a little starter or yogurt, add a spoonful: the bread comes out softer.
⚠ Careful: Never heat wet stones or river stones: they can burst. The pan is very hot — hold it with a cloth. Keep children away from the fire.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.4

Baking in a cast-iron pot in the embers

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour
① Many embers on the lid ② A few embers below ③ Legs or stones keep the pot up ④ The bread inside ⑤ Lid with a rim so embers stay on.
Why: A heavy cast-iron pot with a lid becomes an oven over the fire. You bake bread, stews or pies with no power.
What you need
  • Cast-iron pot with lid (best with legs)
  • Embers from wood or charcoal
  • Small shovel, tongs, thick gloves
  • 3 stones, if the pot has no legs
Step by step
  1. Light a fire 45 minutes before, to make good embers.
  2. Heat the empty pot and lid for 10 minutes.
  3. Put the bread inside on baking paper or a little flour. Close the lid.
  4. Put a few embers underneath and twice as many on the lid.
  5. For a 25–30 cm pot: about 8 coals under, 16 on top (about 200 °C).
  6. Every 15 minutes turn the pot ¼ turn one way and the lid ¼ turn the other.
  7. Bake bread 35–45 minutes. Replace embers when they fade.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Heat rises: that is why most embers go on top. If the bottom burns, put a layer of sand or ash under the pot.
⚠ Careful: NEVER use charcoal or embers inside a house, tent or garage: they make carbon monoxide (an odourless gas that kills). The lid is hot and heavy: lift it with gloves and a hook.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.5

Building a simple clay (mud) oven outside

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 2–3 days work + 1–2 weeks drying
Left: the sand form. Right: the finished oven. ① Stone base ② Fire-brick floor ③ Dome of wet sand (the form) ④ Clay wall, 8–10 cm ⑤ Door ⑥ The fire inside.
Why: A mud oven bakes bread for a whole neighbourhood with little wood. The materials are earth, sand, straw and stones.
What you need
  • Stones or bricks for a base
  • Fire bricks or flat tiles for the floor
  • Clay soil, sand, straw
  • Wet sand for the form, newspaper
  • Buckets, shovel
Step by step
  1. Build a stone base 80–100 cm high, away from houses and trees.
  2. Lay the fire bricks on top, level, on a thin bed of sand.
  3. Make a dome form of wet sand, about 45 cm high. Cover it with wet newspaper.
  4. Mix 1 part clay with 2 parts sand and a little water, like modelling clay.
  5. Press the mix around the form, 8–10 cm thick.
  6. After 1–2 days cut a door about ⅔ of the dome height.
  7. Dig the sand out by hand.
  8. Let it dry 1–2 weeks in shade. Then light small fires for 3–4 days.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Clay test: make a ball and let it dry. If it cracks a lot, add more sand. A second layer of clay mixed with straw keeps the heat for hours.
⚠ Careful: Build it away from dry grass, trees and walls. Do not light it on dry, windy days. Always keep a bucket of water near. Never burn painted or pressed wood: it gives off poisons.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.6

Grinding grain by hand (hand mill) and sifting flour

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour for 1 kg
① Grain poured into the hole ② Top stone (turns) ③ Handle ④ Bottom stone (stays still) ⑤ Flour comes out at the edge ⑥ Sieve holding the bran ⑦ Fine flour in the bowl.
Why: Whole grain keeps for years, flour only a few months. If you have grain and two stones, you have fresh flour.
What you need
  • Wheat, barley or corn, clean and dry
  • Hand mill or two stones (one flat, one round)
  • Sieve
  • Cloth or tray underneath, bowl
Step by step
  1. Winnow the grain in the wind to blow away straw and dust.
  2. Spread it on a tray and pick out small stones and black grains.
  3. Pour a little grain into the hole of the top stone.
  4. Turn the top stone with the handle, steady, at an even pace.
  5. Flour comes out at the edges onto the cloth. Collect it.
  6. Grind it 2–3 times for finer flour.
  7. Sift: fine flour falls into the bowl, the bran stays on top.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: With no mill: put the grain on a flat stone and rub back and forth with a round one. Do not waste the bran — it is good for animals, hens or porridge.
⚠ Careful: Throw away any long black-purple grain (ergot): it is poisonous. Never grind mouldy or damp grain. Wholemeal flour spoils fast: grind only for 1–2 weeks.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.7

Paximadi — twice-baked rusks that last a year

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 day
① Slices 2 cm thick ② Slices standing on the tray in a low oven ③ Low, gentle heat (100–120 °C) ④ Tin with a lid ⑤ Dip in water before eating.
Why: Fresh bread goes mouldy in a few days. A rusk is dry as stone and keeps for months. Sailors and shepherds always carried it.
What you need
  • Loaves of bread (wheat or barley)
  • Sharp knife
  • Oven, or a wood oven that is cooling down
  • Tin with lid or cloth bag
Step by step
  1. Bake bread as usual. Let it cool for 1 hour.
  2. Cut slices 2 cm thick, or cut the loaf in half lengthwise.
  3. Lay the slices on the tray, not touching each other.
  4. Dry them in a low oven, 100–120 °C, for 3–5 hours.
  5. Turn them halfway through.
  6. Break one: it must be dry and hard right to the centre.
  7. Let them cool completely. Store in a tin, in a dry place.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The old way: after baking, put the slices in the cooling wood oven and leave them all night. To eat, dip it quickly in water and add oil, tomato and salt.
⚠ Careful: If the centre stays damp, it will mould. Check the rusks every month; if you see mould, throw that piece away. Very hard rusks can break teeth: soak them first.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.8

Trahanas (sour and sweet) — food that keeps all winter

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour cooking + 1 week drying
① Milk and cracked wheat in the pot ② Low fire, keep stirring ③ Pieces on the sheet ④ Drying in the sun ⑤ Rubbing through the sieve ⑥ Dry crumbs in the jar.
Why: Trahanas locks summer milk into dry crumbs. It keeps for a year and becomes a hot soup in 15 minutes.
What you need
  • 1 kg coarse cracked wheat (bulgur)
  • 2 litres milk: soured milk or thinned yogurt for sour, fresh for sweet
  • 1 tablespoon salt
  • Large pot, wooden spoon
  • Clean sheets, sieve, jars or cloth bags
Step by step
  1. Heat the milk with the salt on a low fire.
  2. Pour in the cracked wheat slowly, stirring all the time.
  3. Cook 20–30 minutes, stirring, until it becomes a thick paste.
  4. Let it cool. Break it into pieces the size of a walnut.
  5. Spread them on a clean sheet in the sun. Cover with net against flies.
  6. Turn them twice a day. Bring them in at night.
  7. After 2–3 days, rub them through a sieve into crumbs.
  8. Spread the crumbs 3–5 more days, until fully dry.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Soup: 1 cup trahanas in 4 cups water or broth, boil 15 minutes. Add cheese or a little butter on top.
⚠ Careful: It must be fully dry before you close it in, or it will mould. If it smells mouldy or you see fuzz, throw the whole batch away. Keep it away from damp and insects (bay leaves in the jar help).
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.9

Homemade pasta — hilopites (egg noodles) and drying

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 morning + 2–3 days drying
① Long thin rolling pin ② Thin sheet of dough ③ Strips 1 cm wide ④ Cut into small squares (hilopites) ⑤ Long strips hung on a pole ⑥ Hilopites on a cloth.
Why: With flour, eggs and milk you make pasta that keeps for months. It is a quick, filling meal for the whole family.
What you need
  • 500 g flour (hard wheat if you have it)
  • 3 eggs
  • 100 ml milk
  • A little salt
  • Long thin rolling pin (or wooden stick), knife
  • Clean cloths, a pole for hanging
Step by step
  1. Mix flour and salt. Put the eggs and milk in the middle.
  2. Knead 10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough. Rest it 30 minutes covered.
  3. Roll a thin sheet, 1–2 mm, with the rolling pin.
  4. Let the sheet dry 20–30 minutes, so it does not stick.
  5. Cut strips 1 cm wide. For hilopites, cut the strips into small squares.
  6. Hang long strips on a pole. Spread the squares on a cloth.
  7. Dry 2–3 days in airy shade. Stir them every day.
  8. When they snap like glass, store them in jars or cloth bags.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: With no eggs: flour, water and salt — plainer, but they keep just as well. Dust the sheet with flour so it does not stick.
⚠ Careful: Egg pasta must dry fully within 2–3 days; if not, cook it the same day. Do not dry it in hot sun: it cracks. If it smells sour or mouldy, throw it away.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.10

Yogurt at home without a machine

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes + 8 hours waiting
① Heat the milk until it rises ② Little-finger test (43–45 °C) ③ A spoon of yogurt as starter ④ Blankets all around ⑤ The pot hidden inside.
Why: Yogurt keeps milk good for more days and is very healthy. One spoon of old yogurt makes new yogurt forever.
What you need
  • 1 litre milk
  • 2 tablespoons yogurt (as starter)
  • Pot or clay bowl, with lid
  • Blankets or old clothes
Step by step
  1. Heat the milk until it starts to rise (85–90 °C). Keep it there 5 minutes.
  2. Take it off the heat and let it cool to 43–45 °C.
  3. Finger test: put in your little finger and count to 10. It should feel hot but bearable.
  4. Mix the 2 spoons of yogurt with a little warm milk in a cup.
  5. Pour it into the pot and stir gently. Close the lid.
  6. Wrap the pot well in blankets. Do not move it for 6–8 hours.
  7. When it has set, put it in a cool place. Keep 2 spoons for next time.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: For thicker yogurt, strain it in a cloth for 2–3 hours. The liquid that drips out is good for bread dough.
⚠ Careful: Always heat the milk first, especially fresh milk from an animal. All tools must be very clean. If the yogurt turns pink, slimy or smells bad, throw it away.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.11

Simple fresh cheese with lemon or vinegar — and using the whey

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Lemon or vinegar into hot milk ② Cheese lumps in the whey ③ Cloth lining the colander ④ Whey collects in the bowl ⑤ Cheese hanging in a cloth to drain.
Why: When you have extra milk, you turn it into cheese in one hour. It is nourishing, and the leftover whey is not wasted.
What you need
  • 2 litres milk (not ultra-heat-treated)
  • Juice of 2 lemons or 4 tablespoons vinegar
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • Colander, clean thin cloth, bowl
  • String
Step by step
  1. Heat the milk, stirring, until it steams and starts to rise (85–90 °C).
  2. Turn off the heat. Add the lemon or vinegar and stir gently.
  3. Wait 10 minutes. White lumps form, plus a yellow-green liquid (whey).
  4. Line the colander with the cloth, over the bowl.
  5. Pour in the lumps. The whey drains into the bowl.
  6. Add the salt and mix.
  7. Tie the cloth and hang it 1–2 hours. For firmer cheese, put a weight on it.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Do not throw away the whey: use it instead of water in bread or soup, drink it cool, or mix 1 part with 4 parts water to water plants.
⚠ Careful: Never drink or use unheated animal milk: it can carry diseases such as brucellosis. Fresh cheese keeps only 3–4 days in a cool place.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.12

Butter from cream in a jar — and clarified butter that keeps

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Jar half full of cream ② Shake up and down ③ Butter ball in cold water ④ Wooden spoon presses out the liquid ⑤ Foam on the melted butter ⑥ Clear golden butter in the jar.
Why: Butter is a precious fat for winter. Clear, clarified butter keeps for months without a fridge.
What you need
  • Cream: skimmed from the top of milk over 1–2 days
  • Glass jar with a good lid
  • Bowl of cold water, wooden spoon
  • Small pot, thin cloth, clean dry jar
Step by step
  1. Fill the jar halfway with cool cream. Close it tight.
  2. Shake hard for 10–20 minutes. First it whips, then you hear a «splash».
  3. It splits into a ball of butter and thin liquid (buttermilk). Keep the buttermilk.
  4. Put the butter in cold water. Press it with the spoon.
  5. Change the water until it stays clear. Add salt if you like (1–2%).
  6. For butter that keeps: melt it on a very low fire for 20–30 minutes.
  7. Skim the foam from the top. White solids sink to the bottom.
  8. Strain the clear golden butter into a dry jar. Close it.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Buttermilk is wonderful in bread, pies and pancakes. Cream turns to butter faster when cool, about 12–15 °C.
⚠ Careful: Melted butter is very hot and can catch fire if overheated: low heat, never pour water on it. Fresh butter needs a cool place and is eaten within days. If it smells rancid, throw it away.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.13

Hay-box (retained-heat cooker) — cooking with almost no fuel

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon to build
① Wooden box ② Hay or blankets, 10 cm all round ③ Pot just off the boil, lid on ④ Pillow on top ⑤ The box lid closes tight.
