Why: You boil the food for a few minutes, then the box finishes cooking it with its own heat. You save more than half your fuel.
What you need
  • Wooden crate, basket or cardboard box with lid
  • Hay, old blankets, clothes or newspaper
  • Pot with a tight-fitting lid
  • A pillow
Step by step
  1. Fill the box with hay or blankets, at least 10 cm all around.
  2. Make a «nest» in the middle, the shape of the pot.
  3. Boil the food with the lid on: rice 5 minutes, beans 15 minutes.
  4. Put the pot quickly into the nest without lifting the lid.
  5. Cover with the pillow and close the box.
  6. Leave it: rice 1–1½ hours, beans 3–4 hours, porridge all night.
  7. Before eating, bring the food back to the boil for a few minutes.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: A full pot holds more heat than a half-empty one. Wrapping the pot in a sleeping bag works the same way.
⚠ Careful: Food must stay above 60 °C. If it cools and stays lukewarm for hours, germs grow: boil it again well. Red kidney beans need 10 minutes of hard boiling first. Never keep hay near a flame.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.14

Solar oven from a box, foil and glass

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2 hours to build
① Outer box ② Insulation (newspaper) ③ Foil lining ④ Glass on top ⑤ Foil reflector ⑥ Black pot on a black floor ⑦ The sun.
Why: The sun is free fuel. On sunny days you cook rice, beans and bread with no wood and no smoke.
What you need
  • 2 cardboard boxes (one fits inside the other)
  • Crumpled newspaper or hay
  • Kitchen foil, glue or tape
  • A sheet of glass (from an old picture frame)
  • Black pot with lid
Step by step
  1. Put the small box inside the big one. Fill the gap (5 cm) with newspaper.
  2. Line the inside of the small box with foil, shiny side out.
  3. Put something black on the floor: a metal sheet, tile or black paper.
  4. Cut a reflector flap from a lid and cover it with foil.
  5. Put the pot inside and the glass on top, closing it well.
  6. Turn the oven to face the sun. Prop the reflector to bounce light inside.
  7. Cook from 10 am to 3 pm. Turn it to the sun every 30–60 minutes.
  8. Times: rice 2 hours, soaked beans 3–5 hours, bread 1½–2 hours.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Two sheets of glass with a small gap keep more heat. An oven thermometer inside shows if you reach 100–150 °C.
⚠ Careful: Do not look into the reflector glare: it hurts the eyes. Glass and pot get very hot: wear gloves. Meat needs over 75 °C for a long time; if the sun goes, finish cooking on a fire.
🍞 Bread & the old-time kitchen · 4.15

Dried beans, lentils, chickpeas: soaking, low-fuel cooking, sprouting — and homemade vinegar

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 day (beans) · 4–8 weeks (vinegar)
① Water three times above the beans ② Net tied over the mouth ③ Jar tilted upside down, draining into a bowl ④ Vinegar «mother» ⑤ Cloth tied on top ⑥ Wine turning into vinegar.
Why: Dried beans keep for years and give protein. Sprouts give fresh vitamins even in winter. Vinegar adds flavour and helps clean.
What you need
  • Beans, lentils, chickpeas
  • Bowl, pot, hay-box if you have one
  • Glass jar, net or gauze, rubber band
  • For vinegar: leftover wine and a little live vinegar with its «mother»
Step by step
  1. Soak beans and chickpeas 12 hours in three times their volume of water. Lentils need none.
  2. Pour off the water, add fresh. Boil hard for 10 minutes.
  3. Simmer with the lid on, or put the pot in a hay-box for 3–4 hours.
  4. Sprouts: soak lentils or chickpeas overnight in a jar. Tie net over the mouth.
  5. Pour off the water. Tilt the jar upside down so it drains.
  6. Rinse twice a day. In 2–4 days you get sprouts 1–2 cm long.
  7. Vinegar: fill a wide jar ¾ with wine and add a little live vinegar.
  8. Cover with a cloth and leave it warm and dark 4–8 weeks, until it smells of strong vinegar.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The slimy skin on top of the vinegar is the «mother»: keep it for the next jar.
⚠ Careful: Red kidney beans are toxic unless boiled hard for 10 minutes — never eat them raw or sprouted. Broad beans: danger for people with favism (G6PD deficiency). Throw away slimy or smelly sprouts. Homemade vinegar may be too weak: do not use it for canning.
Chapter 5

Garden & Seeds

The vegetable garden fed our grandparents without fertiliser and without shops. Here you will learn to build good soil, water with little water and keep your own seeds every year. A seed you save today is next year's food.
  1. Know your soil and make it better
  2. Making compost (fertiliser from scraps)
  3. No-dig raised bed (with cardboard)
  4. Starting seeds in egg cartons and transplanting
  5. Saving tomato, pepper and cucumber seeds
  6. Saving bean, pea, lettuce and herb seeds — and storing them
  7. Watering with a buried clay pot and a bottle
  8. Mulch: less watering, fewer weeds
  9. Plants that help each other
  10. Crop rotation: moving crops every year
  11. Potatoes: the easiest calories
  12. New plants from cuttings
  13. Grafting fruit trees (cleft graft)
  14. Natural pest control
  15. Winter pruning of fruit trees and grapevines
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.1

Know your soil and make it better

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour + 1 day waiting
① Sandy: falls apart ② Good soil: forms a ball ③ Clay: forms a ribbon ④ Sand ⑤ Silt ⑥ Clay ⑦ Plant bits floating ⑧ Worms: sign of living soil
Why: Soil is the foundation of the garden. If you know your soil, you know what it needs.
What you need
  • Spade
  • Glass jar with lid
  • Water
  • A spoon of salt or dish soap
Step by step
  1. Take a handful of moist soil from 10 cm deep and squeeze it in your fist.
  2. If it falls apart, it is sandy. If it forms a ball and breaks when poked, it is good.
  3. If you can roll it into a long ribbon that does not break, it is clay (sticky mud).
  4. Fill the jar 1/3 with soil, top up with water and add a little salt.
  5. Shake hard for 2 minutes and leave it still for one day.
  6. You will see layers: sand at the bottom, silt in the middle, clay on top.
  7. Dig one spadeful and count the worms. More than 5 means living soil.
  8. For every soil the cure is the same: add compost and well-rotted manure every year.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Old farmers said: smell the soil. Good soil smells like a forest after rain. A sour or rotten smell means it is waterlogged.
⚠ Careful: Do not dig near pipes, cables or old dumps. Wear gloves if the soil has glass or rusty metal.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.2

Making compost (fertiliser from scraps)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour to build, 3–6 months to finish
① Brown layer (dry leaves, straw) ② Green layer (peels, grass) ③ A little soil ④ Bin with air gaps ⑤ Stick to check the heat ⑥ Finished compost at the bottom ⑦ Turning with a fork
Why: Without shop fertiliser, compost is the garden's food. It is free, made from peels and leaves.
What you need
  • 4 pallets or planks with gaps
  • Greens: peels, grass, vegetable leaves
  • Browns: dry leaves, straw, cardboard
  • A little soil
  • Fork
  • A wooden stick
Step by step
  1. Set the bin on bare earth, not concrete, in the shade.
  2. Put twigs at the bottom for air. Then a layer of browns, 10 cm.
  3. Add greens on top, 5 cm. Sprinkle a little soil.
  4. Keep layering: about 2 parts browns to 1 part greens.
  5. Keep it damp like a wrung-out sponge. If it dries, water it.
  6. Push a stick into the middle. If it comes out warm, the compost is working.
  7. Every 2–3 weeks turn it with the fork so it gets air.
  8. It is ready when it is dark, crumbly and smells like a forest floor.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: If it smells bad, there are too many greens: add browns. If it stays cold, add greens and water.
⚠ Careful: Do not add meat, fish, dairy, oil, dog or cat droppings, or diseased plants. They bring rats and disease. Wear gloves.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.3

No-dig raised bed (with cardboard)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 morning
① Old grass left in place ② Soaked cardboard ③ Compost 15–20 cm ④ Straw mulch ⑤ Wooden frame ⑥ Plants
Why: Without a tractor or hard work, you build rich soil on top of grass. Roots find soft soil from day one.
What you need
  • Plain cardboard, no tape or print
  • Compost or rotted manure (many barrows)
  • Straw or dry leaves
  • 4 planks or stones for a frame
  • Water
Step by step
  1. Choose a sunny spot, 6+ hours of sun. Cut the grass short.
  2. Do not pull anything out. The weeds will rot underneath.
  3. Lay cardboard with 15 cm overlaps, leaving no gaps.
  4. Water it well until soaked.
  5. Build the frame: up to 1.2 m wide, so you reach the middle without stepping in.
  6. Spread 15–20 cm of compost or rotted manure on the cardboard.
  7. Cover with 5 cm of straw and open holes for the plants.
  8. Plant right away. Every autumn add 5 cm of compost on top.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Never step inside the bed. The soil stays fluffy and the worms do the digging for you.
⚠ Careful: Do not use painted or treated wood (green-tinted, oily, old railway sleepers): it leaks poison into the soil. Fresh manure burns plants: let it rot for 6 months.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.4

Starting seeds in egg cartons and transplanting

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour + 4–8 weeks
① Drainage holes ② Clear cover keeps moisture ③ Seed depth: 2× its size ④ Light from the window ⑤ Hold by a leaf ⑥ Plant a bit deeper
Why: Small plants are fragile. Indoors you protect them from cold and snails and gain a month.
What you need
  • Paper egg cartons or small pots
  • Fine sieved soil or compost
  • Seeds
  • Clear bag or lid
  • Water sprayer
Step by step
  1. Make a small hole in the bottom of each cell for drainage.
  2. Fill with fine soil and water it.
  3. Sow 2 seeds at a depth twice their size.
  4. Cover with a clear bag and keep warm, 18–25 °C.
  5. Once they sprout, remove the bag and move them to a bright window.
  6. Keep the strongest plant. Snip the other with scissors.
  7. One week before, put them outside a few hours a day to toughen up.
  8. Plant in the evening. Hold the plant by a leaf, not the stem. Water.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Plant tomatoes deep, up to the first leaves. They grow roots along the buried stem and get stronger.
⚠ Careful: Bought seeds may be coated with chemicals: wash your hands and keep them away from children and animals.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.5

Saving tomato, pepper and cucumber seeds

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 20 min + 3 days fermenting + 1 week drying
① Scoop seeds with juice ② Mould on top after 2–4 days ③ Good seeds sink ④ Rinse in a sieve ⑤ Dry on a plate, in the shade
Why: With your own seeds you never need a shop again. Each year the plant also adapts to your place.
What you need
  • Ripe fruit from the best plants
  • Small jar
  • Spoon
  • Sieve
  • Plate
  • Paper envelope
Step by step
  1. Pick tomatoes from healthy, traditional plants (local varieties, not hybrids).
  2. Cut the tomato and scoop out the seeds with their juice.
  3. Put them in a jar with a little water. Cover with a cloth.
  4. Leave 2–4 days. Mould will form on top: this cleans the seeds.
  5. Good seeds sink to the bottom. Throw away what floats.
  6. Rinse in the sieve and spread on a plate, in the shade, for 7 days.
  7. Pepper: take seeds from a ripe red pepper and dry them straight away.
  8. Cucumber: let it turn yellow on the plant, then treat it like tomato.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Save seeds from 5–6 different plants, not just one. This keeps the seeds strong for years.
⚠ Careful: Seeds from hybrids (F1) do not grow true. Do not dry on kitchen paper (they stick) or in an oven or hot sun (they die).
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.6

Saving bean, pea, lettuce and herb seeds — and storing them

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Dry pods on the plant ② Shelled seeds ③ Fluff on flowering lettuce ④ Shake into a paper bag ⑤ Jar with tight lid ⑥ Cloth with dry rice ⑦ Label: name and year
Why: Beans and peas are the easiest seeds. They are also protein for the table. Well-stored seeds last 3–5 years.
What you need
  • Paper bags
  • Glass jars with tight lids
  • A little dry rice in a cloth
  • Paper labels and pencil
Step by step
  1. Leave some beans and peas on the plant until the pod is dry and rattles.
  2. Pick on a dry day. Shell the pods and spread the seeds for 2 weeks in the shade.
  3. Lettuce: let one plant flower. When it shows white fluff, cut the top.
  4. Put the top upside down in a paper bag and shake. The seeds fall in.
  5. Herbs (dill, basil, parsley): cut dry flower heads into a bag and shake.
  6. Test: a dry seed snaps, it does not bend.
  7. Put the seeds in a jar with a cloth of dry rice to soak up moisture.
  8. Write name and year. Store in a cool, dark place.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: For beans: put the jar in the freezer for 3 days. It kills weevil eggs that bore into the seeds.
⚠ Careful: Never seal seeds in a jar unless fully dry: they go mouldy. Raw beans are toxic: eat them only well boiled.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.7

Watering with a buried clay pot and a bottle

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Lid (stone or saucer) ② Unglazed pot full of water ③ Water seeps through the clay ④ Roots grow to the pot ⑤ Bottle upside down, bottom cut off ⑥ Cap with small holes ⑦ Roots
Why: When water is scarce, every drop counts. A buried clay pot waters the roots and wastes far less than a hose.
What you need
  • Unglazed clay pot or jar (not shiny)
  • Cork and waterproof sealant for the hole
  • Stone or saucer as a lid
  • 1.5-litre plastic bottles
  • Nail
Step by step
  1. If the pot has a hole in the bottom, seal it with cork and sealant.
  2. Bury it up to the neck, among 3–4 plants, 30–40 cm away.
  3. Fill it with water and cover with a stone, against dirt and mosquitoes.
  4. Water seeps slowly through the clay and the roots grow towards it.
  5. Refill when empty, every 2–5 days.
  6. Bottle: make 2–3 small holes in the cap with a hot nail.
  7. Cut off the bottle's bottom. Bury it upside down, cap 15 cm deep.
  8. Fill it from the top. It drips slowly to the roots.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Always water morning or evening, never midday. Cover the soil with mulch: it keeps water twice as long.
⚠ Careful: Heat the nail holding it with pliers, not your fingers. Always cover water: open containers breed mosquitoes and can drown small children.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.8

Mulch: less watering, fewer weeds

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Bare soil: dries and cracks ② Weeds ③ Water lost to the sun ④ Straw 5–10 cm ⑤ Gap around the stem ⑥ Moist soil with worms
Why: Bare soil dries, hardens and fills with weeds. Covered, it holds water and feeds the worms.
What you need
  • Straw, dry leaves, cut grass or wood chips
  • Rake
  • Water
Step by step
  1. Weed first and water the soil well.
  2. Spread straw or dry leaves 5–10 cm thick.
  3. Leave a 5 cm gap around each stem so it does not rot.
  4. Use fresh grass clippings thin, 2–3 cm, or they heat up and smell.
  5. Use wood chips on paths and under trees, not on small vegetables.
  6. Top up when it gets thin. What rots becomes soil.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Lift the straw on a hot afternoon: the soil underneath will be damp and cool. That is all the magic.
⚠ Careful: Snails hide in mulch, and in warm places sometimes snakes or scorpions: wear gloves. Do not use weeds with seeds or grass sprayed with weedkiller. Keep dry straw away from fire.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.9

Plants that help each other

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon of sowing
① Corn: the pole ② Climbing bean ③ Squash leaves give shade ④ Mound with compost ⑤ Tomato ⑥ Basil
Why: You get more food from the same space. The right plant partners protect and feed each other.
What you need
  • Corn seeds
  • Climbing bean seeds
  • Squash or pumpkin seeds
  • Tomato and basil plants
  • Compost
Step by step
  1. Three sisters: make a low mound, 1 m wide, with compost inside.
  2. Sow 4–6 corn in the middle, 25 cm apart, after the last frost.
  3. When they reach 15 cm, sow one bean next to each corn.
  4. The bean climbs the corn and adds nitrogen (plant food) to the soil.
  5. Sow 2 squash at the edge. The big leaves shade the soil and stop weeds.
  6. Plant basil between tomatoes. Its smell keeps insects away.
  7. Put marigolds (flowers) along the garden edges to bring bees.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Bad partners: beans with onions or garlic, and potatoes with tomatoes (they share diseases).
⚠ Careful: If you sow the bean too early, it smothers the corn. Let the corn grow first.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.10

Crop rotation: moving crops every year

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: A few minutes of planning a year
① Legumes ② Leafy greens ③ Fruiting crops ④ Roots. Arrows show where each group goes next year
Why: If you grow the same crop in the same spot, the soil tires and collects diseases. With 4 beds that rotate, it stays healthy without sprays.
What you need
  • 4 beds of about the same size
  • A notebook
  • Compost
Step by step
  1. Divide the garden into 4 beds and number them 1–4.
  2. Bed 1: legumes (beans, peas, broad beans). They leave nitrogen in the soil.
  3. Bed 2: leafy greens (cabbage, lettuce, spinach). They use the nitrogen.
  4. Bed 3: fruiting crops (tomato, pepper, aubergine, courgette). Give them compost.
  5. Bed 4: roots (carrot, potato, onion, beetroot).
  6. Each year every group moves one bed forward, clockwise.
  7. Write in the notebook what you planted where, every year.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Tomato, potato, pepper and aubergine are relatives. Do not plant any of them where another one grew last year.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.11

Potatoes: the easiest calories

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 2 hours planting, 3–4 months to harvest
① Potato with short green sprouts ② Chitting in an egg tray ③ Seed potato 10–15 cm deep ④ Earthed-up mound ⑤ Sack with soil ⑥ Add soil as it grows
Why: Potatoes give more food per metre than grain. One seed potato gives 6–10 potatoes.
What you need
  • Seed potatoes (healthy, small, or pieces with 2 eyes)
  • Egg trays
  • Hoe
  • Compost
  • Strong sack or big tub with holes
Step by step
  1. Put the potatoes in egg trays, in light and cool air, 3–4 weeks.
  2. They grow short green sprouts. This is called chitting.
  3. Dig a trench 10–15 cm deep. Place potatoes every 30 cm, sprouts up.
  4. Cover with soil and compost. Keep rows 60–70 cm apart.
  5. When plants reach 20 cm, pull soil around them into a mound (earthing up).
  6. Sack: put 15 cm of soil, 3 potatoes, and add soil as the plant grows.
  7. Harvest when the leaves die back. Leave them 2 hours in shade to dry.
  8. Store in a dark, cool place, in a crate, not a plastic bag.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Keep the best small potatoes as seed for next year. Do not eat them in winter.
⚠ Careful: Never eat green potatoes, sprouts, leaves or the small green fruits of the plant: they are poisonous (solanine). That is why you earth up: potatoes in light turn green.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.12

New plants from cuttings

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour + 2–4 months to root
① Last year's wood, pencil-thick, 20–25 cm ② Straight cut below a bud ③ Slanted cut above a bud ④ 1–2 buds stay above soil ⑤ Pot with sandy soil ⑥ New leaves ⑦ New roots
Why: From one fig tree or vine you make dozens of free new plants, identical to the mother. No nursery needed.
What you need
  • Clean sharp pruning shears
  • Pot with a hole
  • Half sand, half soil
  • Water
Step by step
  1. Cut in winter, when the tree has no leaves (fig, grape, pomegranate).
  2. Choose last year's branch, pencil-thick, 20–25 cm long.
  3. At the bottom cut straight, just below a bud.
  4. At the top cut at a slant, 1 cm above a bud. This shows which end is up.
  5. Push 2/3 of the cutting into moist sandy soil. Leave 1–2 buds above.
  6. Keep the soil moist, not muddy, in half shade.
  7. Rosemary: cut 10 cm tips in spring, strip the lower leaves and plant.
  8. Transplant next autumn, when you see new leaves and roots.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Put 3 cuttings in each pot. If all three root, you have gifts for the neighbours.
⚠ Careful: Fig sap burns skin in sunlight: wear gloves and long sleeves. Close the shears after use.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.13

Grafting fruit trees (cleft graft)

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 30 minutes per tree
① Scion with 2–3 buds ② Wedge cut 3–4 cm ③ Split in the stump ④ Scion's green layer touches the tree's ⑤ Tie ⑥ Wax on top
Why: Grafting turns a wild or poor tree into one with good fruit. Our grandparents grafted wild pears and wild cherries.
What you need
  • Sharp grafting knife
  • Pruning saw
  • Scions: twigs from a good tree
  • Wedge or screwdriver
  • Grafting tape or raffia
  • Grafting wax or beeswax
Step by step
  1. Cut scions in January, pencil-thick. Keep them in damp sand in the fridge.
  2. Graft at the end of winter, when the tree's buds start to swell.
  3. Saw the tree branch off straight, 3–8 cm thick.
  4. Split the stump in the middle with the knife, 5 cm deep. Hold it open with the wedge.
  5. Cut each scion into a wedge 3–4 cm long, with 2–3 buds above.
  6. Put one scion at each edge. The green layer under the bark must touch.
  7. Remove the wedge. The wood squeezes the scions. Tie tightly.
  8. Wax the top, the split and the scion tips, so no water gets in.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Graft only relatives: pear on pear or quince, cherry on cherry, plum on plum or peach.
⚠ Careful: Always cut away from your body and fingers. A grafting knife is very sharp. Never put a finger into the split.
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.14

Natural pest control

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: A few minutes every day
① Soapy water in the sprayer ② Aphids under the leaf ③ Bucket of nettles ④ Picking a caterpillar by hand ⑤ Ash ring against snails ⑥ Birds: the garden's guards
Why: When there are no sprays, simple means and a daily look save the garden. They are healthier for you too.
What you need
  • Sprayer
  • Plain olive-oil soap
  • Bucket
  • Nettles
  • Wood ash
  • Gloves
Step by step
  1. Walk the garden every morning. Turn leaves and look underneath.
  2. Aphids (tiny green insects): spray 1 spoon of grated soap in 1 litre of water.
  3. Spray in the evening, not in sun. Repeat every 3 days.
  4. Nettle tea: 1 kg nettles in 10 litres of water, covered, 2 weeks.
  5. Strain it, dilute 1 to 10 and water the plants. It makes them stronger.
  6. Caterpillars and beetles: pick them by hand into a bucket of soapy water.
  7. Snails: put a ring of dry ash around the plant. Renew after rain.
  8. Hang bird boxes and leave a dish of water. Birds eat thousands of insects.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Ladybirds eat aphids. Do not kill them and do not spray when you see them.
⚠ Careful: Wear gloves for nettles. Nettle tea stinks: keep it away from the house. Use ash only from clean wood, not painted wood or barbecue charcoal, and do not handle it with wet hands (it burns).
🌱 Garden & Seeds · 5.15

Winter pruning of fruit trees and grapevines

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 hours per tree
① Dead branch ② Crossing branches ③ Water shoot ④ Sucker at the base ⑤ Open middle like a bowl ⑥ Vine: cut the cane back to 2 buds ⑦ The vine's old arm ⑧ Slanted cut above a bud. Red lines: where to cut
Why: A well-pruned tree gives bigger fruit and gets sick less. An unpruned vine gives only leaves.
What you need
  • Sharp pruning shears
  • Pruning saw
  • Gloves
  • Steady ladder
  • Alcohol for cleaning
Step by step
  1. Prune in January–February, on a dry day, without frost.
  2. First cut dead and diseased branches.
  3. Then branches that cross or rub each other.
  4. Cut water shoots (straight up-growing shoots) and suckers at the base.
  5. Open the tree's middle like a bowl, so sun and air get in.
  6. Cut at a slant, 0.5–1 cm above a bud that faces outwards.
  7. Vine: on each of this year's canes leave only 2 buds (a spur).
  8. Clean the shears with alcohol between trees.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Never remove more than 1/3 of a tree in one year. Old growers said: prune a little, prune every year.
⚠ Careful: Set the ladder on firm ground and have someone hold it. Never prune near power lines. Always cut away from your body.
Chapter 6

Animals, Fishing & Food from nature

Our grandparents kept a few hens, a goat and a beehive. They fished with a hand line and gathered wild greens, snails and herbs. Here you will learn these simple skills, with respect for animals, nature and the law.
  1. A small hen house: perch, nest box, fox-proof
  2. Keeping hens for eggs: food, water, care
  3. Hatching chicks with a broody hen (21 days)
  4. Keeping rabbits (hutch, food, cleanliness)
  5. Keeping a goat, milking by hand, boiling milk
  6. Bees: the hive and taking honey safely
  7. Fishing with a hand line and hook
  8. Bottle trap for small fish (only where legal)
  9. Cleaning fish and cooking on a stick or stone
  10. Wild greens of Greece
  11. Collecting snails after rain and purging them
  12. Acorns, carobs and wild fruits as food
  13. Collecting and drying wild herbs
  14. Mushrooms: the golden rule
  15. Making sea salt from clean sea water
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.1

A small hen house: perch, nest box, fox-proof

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2–3 days
① perch ② nest box with straw ③ door with ramp (shut at night) ④ high vent ⑤ run with strong mesh ⑥ mesh buried 30 cm and bent outwards
Why: A few hens give fresh eggs every day. But they need a dry, safe house, or a fox or marten will take them.
What you need
  • wood and boards
  • tiles or metal sheet for the roof
  • welded wire mesh (13 mm holes)
  • nails, screws, hinges, a bolt
  • straw
Step by step
  1. Pick a dry spot, shaded in summer. For 5 hens build a house about 1 × 1.2 m.
  2. Raise the floor 40–50 cm off the ground, against damp and mice.
  3. Give the roof a slope so rain runs off. Leave a high vent covered with mesh.
  4. Fit a perch (round wood, 4–5 cm thick) 50–60 cm high. Allow 25 cm per hen.
  5. Make a nest box 30 × 30 cm in a dark corner. One box per 4 hens. Add straw.
  6. Make a small door with a ramp. Bolt it shut every evening.
  7. Fence a run of 1–2 m² per hen. Bury the mesh 30 cm deep and bend it outwards.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A fox digs under the fence. Mesh bent outwards under the soil stops it.
⚠ Careful: Foxes tear thin chicken wire; use strong welded mesh. Watch for sticking-out nails. Wash your hands after cleaning.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.2

Keeping hens for eggs: food, water, care

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes a day
① drinker with clean water ② feeder with grain ③ bowl of crushed shells ④ dust-bath hollow ⑤ greens
Why: A good hen lays 4–6 eggs a week. She eats scraps and weeds and gives manure for the garden.
What you need
  • a clean drinker
  • a feeder
  • wheat, maize, barley
  • eggshells or sea shells
  • sand or ash for a dust bath
Step by step
  1. Give each hen about 120 g of grain a day, about one cup.
  2. Add greens, vegetable peels and crumbs. No mouldy or salty food.
  3. Change the water every day. A hen drinks about half a litre a day.
  4. Bake eggshells in the oven, crush them and put them in a separate bowl. They make strong shells.
  5. Leave a corner with dry soil or ash. Hens bathe there and get rid of lice.
  6. Collect eggs every day. Change the straw when it gets dirty.
  7. Look at your hens daily. Put a tired hen with puffed-up feathers on her own.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: In winter, with less daylight, hens lay fewer eggs. This is normal, not illness.
⚠ Careful: Wash your hands after touching hens or eggs (salmonella). Do not wash eggs before storing. Cook eggs well. Never feed mouldy food.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.3

Hatching chicks with a broody hen (21 days)

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 21 days
① broody hen on the nest ② egg in torchlight with veins: alive ③ clear egg: remove ④ chick on day 21 ⑤ shallow water with pebbles
Why: With a broody hen you need no power and no incubator. Your flock renews itself every year.
What you need
  • a broody hen
  • 10–12 fertile eggs (a rooster is needed)
  • a quiet nest
  • a pencil
  • a torch
  • a shallow dish, pebbles
Step by step
  1. A broody hen will not leave the nest and clucks. Give her 2 days to show it.
  2. Choose clean eggs, up to 10 days old. Mark them with pencil.
  3. Put them under her in the evening. Keep water and feed near the nest.
  4. On day 7, in the dark, shine the torch through each egg. Little veins mean it is alive.
  5. Remove eggs that are fully clear. They will not hatch.
  6. From day 18 do not disturb her. Chicks hatch on days 19–22.
  7. Do not help a chick out of the shell. You will usually harm it.
  8. Give water in a shallow dish with pebbles, and finely ground maize or wheat.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Marked eggs help you remove new eggs other hens lay in the same nest.
⚠ Careful: Chicks drown easily in deep water; always add pebbles. Keep cats and dogs away. Wash your hands.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.4

Keeping rabbits (hutch, food, cleanliness)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes a day
① sleeping box ② wire front ③ hay rack ④ water bottle ⑤ droppings tray ⑥ legs 50 cm
Why: Rabbits eat mostly grass and hay, breed quickly and give meat and manure for the garden.
What you need
  • a hutch about 1.5 × 0.6 × 0.6 m per adult
  • hay
  • greens and vegetables
  • a water bottle
  • a droppings tray
Step by step
  1. Set the hutch in shade, 50 cm off the ground, away from rain and wind.
  2. Make a closed dark sleeping box and a part with a wire front.
  3. Give unlimited hay. It is 80% of their food.
  4. Give a handful of dry greens or vegetables daily. Change food slowly.
  5. Clean water always. In summer a rabbit drinks up to half a litre.
  6. Empty the tray every day. The droppings go straight onto the garden.
  7. Separate males from females at 3 months, or they will breed out of control.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Rabbit droppings can go on the garden without composting. They do not burn plants.
⚠ Careful: Never lift a rabbit by its ears. Above 28 °C it risks heatstroke. No wet, sprayed or mouldy greens.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.5

Keeping a goat, milking by hand, boiling milk

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 20 minutes, twice a day
① teat on the udder ② clean bucket ③ straining through cheesecloth ④ boiling the milk ⑤ fire
Why: A goat gives 1–3 litres of milk a day. She eats shrubs and grass and needs little.
What you need
  • a goat that has kidded
  • a pen with a roof
  • a clean stainless bucket
  • cheesecloth
  • a cooking pot
Step by step
  1. Give a dry pen, water always, hay, grazing and a salt lick.
  2. Before milking, wash your hands and wipe the udder with warm water.
  3. Throw away the first 2 squirts from each teat. That is where germs are.
  4. Close the top of the teat with thumb and finger. Then squeeze the other fingers, top to bottom.
  5. Milk calmly, morning and evening, at the same time each day.
  6. Strain the milk through cheesecloth at once.
  7. Boil it: let it rise and keep it 2–3 minutes, stirring. Then cool it fast.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: If the goat kicks, give her a little grain to eat while you milk.
⚠ Careful: Never drink raw milk: it can carry brucellosis (Malta fever). Always boil. Hot, hard udder or lumpy milk: do not drink it, call a vet.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.6

Bees: the hive and taking honey safely

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 1 morning (harvest)
① roof ② honey box ③ brood box ④ entrance ⑤ frame with capped honey ⑥ smoker
Why: Honey never spoils and is a sweet food. Bees also pollinate your garden.
What you need
  • a hive with frames
  • a suit with veil and gloves
  • a smoker with dry leaves or sacking
  • a hive tool
  • a knife, a sieve, jars
Step by step
  1. Learn from a beekeeper. The bottom box is the brood (young), the top box holds honey.
  2. Face the entrance to morning sun, away from roads and houses.
  3. Harvest on a warm calm morning. Wear the full suit.
  4. Give 2–3 gentle puffs of smoke at the entrance. Wait 1 minute.
  5. Open slowly. Take only frames whose honey is three-quarters capped with wax.
  6. Leave the brood box and 15–20 kg of honey for winter.
  7. Cut off the wax caps, let the honey drain through a sieve and fill clean jars.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Move slowly. Bees get angry at quick moves and strong smells.
⚠ Careful: Sting allergy (swollen face, hard breathing) = call emergency (112) at once. Allergic people stay away from hives. Do not over-smoke: it burns bees. No honey for babies under 1 year.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.7

Fishing with a hand line and hook

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1–3 hours
① winder ② line ③ baited hook ④ sinker ⑤ knot with 5 turns ⑥ wet it and pull tight
Why: The sea gives food all year. With a line and a few hooks you can fish without a rod.
What you need
  • fishing line 0.25–0.30 mm
  • hooks size 10–12
  • a sinker 20–40 g
  • a wooden winder
  • bait: worm, shrimp, bread
Step by step
  1. Wind 20–30 m of line onto the winder.
  2. Tie the sinker at the end. 30 cm above it, tie a short side line with the hook.
  3. Knot: pass the line through the hook eye, wrap it 5 times round itself, then pass the end back through the first loop.
  4. Wet the knot with spit and pull tight. Cut off the spare end.
  5. Put bait on so it covers the whole hook.
  6. Cast from a rock or pier, near stones and seaweed. Best times: dawn and dusk.
  7. Hold the line on one finger. When you feel a tug, jerk once and pull in steadily.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Find worms under stones on the shore or by digging in wet sand.
⚠ Careful: Puffer fish (it blows up like a ball) is deadly: never eat it. Weever and scorpion fish sting with spines. Beware slippery rocks. Follow local fishing rules and release small fish.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.8

Bottle trap for small fish (only where legal)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes + a few hours
Top: cut at the red line and turn the neck around. ① funnel pointing in ② bait ③ small holes ④ string to the shore ⑤ stone for weight
Why: A plastic bottle catches small fish and shrimp for bait or for the pan.
What you need
  • a 1.5–2 litre plastic bottle
  • a knife or scissors
  • a nail for holes
  • string
  • a stone
  • bait: bread, fish scraps
Step by step
  1. First ask the port authority or council. In many places traps are banned for amateurs.
  2. Cut the bottle where the neck starts to narrow.
  3. Turn the neck around and push it inside like a funnel. Tie it with string in two places.
  4. Make 8–10 small holes with a hot nail, so air escapes and it sinks.
  5. Put bait and a small stone inside.
  6. Set it in shallow calm water, funnel facing the current. Tie the string to a rock.
  7. Check it every 1–2 hours. Let very small fish go.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Bread dough mixed with a little cheese smells strong and brings fish quickly.
⚠ Careful: Never leave the trap forgotten: it kills animals for nothing and pollutes. Always take the bottle home. Watch the sharp cut edges.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.9

Cleaning fish and cooking on a stick or stone

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① scrape scales tail to head ② cut the belly ③ guts out ④ fish on a green stick, leaning ⑤ embers
Why: Fish spoils fast. Clean it at once and cook it well, and it is safe and tasty.
What you need
  • a sharp knife
  • a board or flat stone
  • clean water
  • a green stick or flat stone
  • salt
Step by step
  1. Scrape off the scales with the back of the knife, from tail to head.
  2. Cut the belly from the small vent hole to the gills. Do not push the blade deep.
  3. Pull out the guts and gills with your fingers.
  4. Rinse well inside and out. Bury the guts or keep them as bait.
  5. Salt it. Push a green stick (never oleander) through the mouth.
  6. Lean the stick over embers, not in the flame. Turn every 3–4 minutes.
  7. Or heat a flat stone in the fire for 30 minutes and cook on it.
  8. It is done when the flesh is white and comes off the bone.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Clear eyes, red gills and firm flesh mean a fresh fish.
⚠ Careful: Always cut away from your body. River or wet stones can burst in fire: use only dry stone. Oleander is poisonous. Never eat puffer fish.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.10

Wild greens of Greece

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 hours
① dandelion/chicory ② amaranth ③ purslane ④ nettle ⑤ spiny chicory ⑥ wild asparagus ⑦ HEMLOCK – deadly ⑧ SPURGE – milky sap, no
Why: Wild greens are free, full of vitamins and grow everywhere from autumn to spring.
What you need
  • a small knife
  • a cloth bag
  • gloves (for nettles)
  • a local person who knows
Step by step
  1. Learn the plants in the field with a local person. Pick only what you know 100%.
  2. Dandelion/chicory: rosette of toothed leaves, yellow flower, milky sap. Amaranth: upright, oval leaves, summer.
  3. Purslane: thick fleshy leaves, reddish stems, NO milky sap. Can be eaten raw.
  4. Nettle: heart-shaped toothed leaves that sting. Pick the tops with gloves.
  5. Spiny chicory: a thorny 'ball'; eat its winter rosette. Wild asparagus: tender spring shoots.
  6. Cut with a knife, leave the root. Do not take all plants from one spot.
  7. Wash in 3 waters. Boil 5–10 minutes (nettles always).
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Greens are most tender before they flower.
⚠ Careful: Hemlock (white umbrella flowers, red spots on stem, nasty smell) kills. Mandrake and other plants look like greens. Spurge looks like purslane but has milky sap. Never pick by roads or sprayed fields. Poisoning: call emergency (Greece 210 7793777).
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.11

Collecting snails after rain and purging them

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour + 7 days
① live snail after rain ② bucket with mesh lid ③ flour and thyme ④ boiling 10–15 minutes
Why: Many snails come out after rain. They are good protein if cleaned properly.
What you need
  • a bucket or box with holes
  • mesh for a lid
  • flour or bran
  • thyme
  • salt, vinegar
  • a pot
Step by step
  1. Collect at night or in the morning after rain. Only big ones, with a hard shell lip.
  2. Not from roads, rubbish or sprayed fields.
  3. Put them in a bucket with holes and a mesh lid, in a cool place.
  4. For 5 days feed flour and thyme. Spray a little water. Clean daily.
  5. Give nothing for the last 2 days, so they empty out.
  6. Throw away dead ones: they do not move when touched or smell bad.
  7. Wash in water with salt and vinegar, rinse 3 times.
  8. Boil them for at least 10–15 minutes before any recipe.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Sealed summer snails (with a thin film over the opening) are already clean.
⚠ Careful: Never raw or half-cooked: they carry parasites. Wash your hands. Dead snails can poison you. Take only a few, leave some for next year.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.12

Acorns, carobs and wild fruits as food

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 weeks (leaching)
① acorn and shelled kernel ② carob pod ③ chopped kernels in water ④ grinding into flour ⑤ change the water every day
Why: Oaks and carob trees grow everywhere. Prepared right, their fruit becomes flour and sweetener.
What you need
  • acorns without holes
  • ripe brown carob pods
  • a big jar
  • clean water
  • a mortar or mill
Step by step
  1. Gather acorns in autumn. Throw away any with holes or that float in water.
  2. Crack the shell and take out the kernel. Chop it small.
  3. Put it in a jar of cold water. The water turns brown from tannins (bitterness).
  4. Change the water every day, for 7–14 days, until no longer bitter.
  5. Faster: boil them and change the water 5–8 times, until it stays clear.
  6. Dry in the sun or a warm oven. Grind into flour for bread or biscuits.
  7. Carobs: eat the flesh raw. Throw away the hard seeds. Boiled, they make a syrup.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Other wild fruits: blackberries, prickly pears (burn off the spines), strawberry-tree fruit (only a few, they make you dizzy).
⚠ Careful: Raw bitter acorns harm the kidneys and stomach: always leach them. Never eat unknown berries: many are poisonous (e.g. ivy).
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.13

Collecting and drying wild herbs

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 morning + 1–2 weeks
① cut at the red line (top third) ② small tied bunch ③ hung upside down in shade ④ glass jar ⑤ the root stays
Why: Oregano, thyme, sage and mountain tea flavour food and make warm drinks in winter.
What you need
  • scissors or a small knife
  • string
  • a shady airy place
  • glass jars with lids
  • paper for labels
Step by step
  1. Pick just before all flowers open (May–July), in the morning once the dew dries.
  2. Cut only the top third of the plant. Never pull up roots.
  3. Take a little from many plants, not all from one. Pick only for your home.
  4. Shake off insects and soil. Do not wash.
  5. Tie small bunches, as thick as your thumb.
  6. Hang them upside down in shade and air, 1–2 weeks. Not in the sun.
  7. When they crumble in your fingers, store in a labelled, dated glass jar.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Herbs keep their scent for one year. After that, burn them to scent the house.
⚠ Careful: Only plants you know for sure. Large amounts of sage are not for pregnant women or epileptics. Traditional use only, not instead of a doctor. Large harvests need a permit.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.14

Mushrooms: the golden rule

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: —
Death cap: ① cap ② white gills ③ ring ④ 'cup' hidden in the soil ⑤ never on the plate without an expert ⑥ if poisoned: doctor at once
Why: One wrong mushroom can kill a whole family. The rule is simple: never eat a mushroom unless an expert confirms it.
What you need
  • a basket (not a bag)
  • a small knife
  • an experienced mushroom expert or club
Step by step
  1. Golden rule: if you are not 100% sure, you DO NOT eat it. Ever.
  2. The death cap (green-white cap, white gills, a ring, a 'cup' at the base) is the deadliest.
  3. Lift the whole mushroom with its base. The 'cup' hides in the soil.
  4. Keep each kind separate in the basket. One poisonous one spoils the rest.
  5. Show them to an expert, one by one, before cooking.
  6. The 'tricks' do not work: silver spoon, garlic, peeling, 'animals ate it' – all false.
  7. Throw away old, soft or wormy ones.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Buy, or learn from a mushroom club. At first, learn 2–3 safe kinds very well.
⚠ Careful: Death cap symptoms come 6–24 hours later, then seem to pass while the liver is destroyed. If someone ate an unknown mushroom: call emergency (112) or poison control (Greece 210 7793777) at once; keep a piece.
🐓 Animals, Fishing & Food from nature · 6.15

Making sea salt from clean sea water

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 3–10 days in the sun
① water from clean sea ② straining through cloth ③ shallow tray in the sun ④ salt drying in a bowl
Why: Without salt you cannot preserve meat, fish, olives or cheese. The sea gives it for free.
What you need
  • clean buckets
  • cotton cloth for a filter
  • wide shallow trays (not aluminium)
  • a wooden spatula
  • a glass jar
Step by step
  1. Take water from open, clean sea. Far from ports, river mouths and sewage outlets.
  2. Let it stand 1 hour so sand settles.
  3. Strain it through a double cloth.
  4. Fill shallow trays only 2–3 cm deep. Cover with net against dust and insects.
  5. Leave them in the sun. In 3–10 days the water goes and salt is left.
  6. Faster: boil in a pot until little water is left, then let it dry.
  7. Collect the crystals with a wooden spatula. Dry for 1 day and store in a glass jar.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: 10 litres of sea water give about 300–350 g of salt.
⚠ Careful: Dirty water gives dirty salt: boiling does not remove oil or chemicals. Never leave a fire unattended. Throw away the bitter liquid left at the end.
Chapter 7

Herbs & Home Care

Our grandmothers always kept herbs in the cupboard and knew how to make soap and salve. Here you will find simple, traditional and safe recipes for small problems and for keeping clean. They do not replace a doctor: if something is serious or not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor or pharmacist.
  1. Infusion and decoction: making herbal tea properly
  2. Drying and storing herbs
  3. Chamomile: tea and compress
  4. Sage and thyme for sore throat and cough
  5. Mountain tea, linden and mint
  6. Calendula salve with olive oil and beeswax
  7. St John's wort oil (red oil)
  8. Honey on small wounds; garlic and onion
  9. Oxymel (vinegar and honey)
  10. Home oral rehydration solution for diarrhoea
  11. Cleaning teeth without toothpaste
  12. Keeping mosquitoes, fleas and lice away
  13. Olive oil soap (cold process)
  14. Cleaning and disinfecting without shop products
  15. Aloe and cool water for minor burns
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.1

Infusion and decoction: making herbal tea properly

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 10–20 minutes
Left, infusion: ① water just off the boil ② leaves and flowers in the cup ③ saucer as a lid ④ 5–10 minutes. Right, decoction: ⑤ roots and bark in the water ⑥ low fire ⑦ 10–20 minutes.
Why: A properly made tea draws out the good of the herb without spoiling it. You only need water, fire and a cover.
What you need
  • Dried or fresh herb
  • Water
  • Kettle or small pot
  • Cup and a saucer as a lid
  • Strainer
Step by step
  1. For leaves and flowers make an infusion (steeping in hot water).
  2. Put 1 teaspoon dried herb (or 1 tablespoon fresh) in a cup.
  3. Pour 250 ml of water that has just stopped boiling.
  4. Cover with a saucer for 5–10 minutes so the aroma stays in.
  5. For roots, bark and seeds make a decoction (boiling).
  6. Put 1 teaspoon in 300 ml cold water and bring it to the boil.
  7. Lower the heat and simmer, covered, for 10–20 minutes.
  8. Strain and drink warm. Keep the rest cool for up to 24 hours.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The drops under the saucer hold the herb's oils. Tip them back into the cup.
⚠ Careful: Only pick plants you know for sure — many poisonous plants look harmless. Usually up to 2–3 cups a day. If pregnant, breastfeeding, for small children or if you take medicines, ask a doctor or pharmacist first. If you are not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.2

Drying and storing herbs

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1–2 weeks
① small bunch tied with string ② moving air and shade ③ paper bag with holes ④ glass jar with a tight lid ⑤ label with name and date.
Why: Herbs grow for only a few months a year. Dried well, they give you tea and remedies all winter.
What you need
  • Scissors or small knife
  • String
  • Paper bags
  • Glass jars with lids
  • Labels and a pencil
Step by step
  1. Cut herbs in the morning, after the dew dries, on a day without rain.
  2. Take only healthy stems. Shake them; do not wash them if clean.
  3. Tie small bunches of 5–10 stems each.
  4. Hang them upside down in the shade, in a cool, airy place.
  5. If there is dust or flies, cover with a paper bag with small holes.
  6. In 1–2 weeks the leaves crumble in your fingers: they are ready.
  7. Put the leaves in a dry glass jar, closed, in a dark cupboard.
  8. Write a label with name and date. Keep them up to 1 year.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Do not dry them in the sun: they lose colour and scent. If they still smell strong, they are good.
⚠ Careful: Do not pick near roads, sprayed fields or rubbish. Only pick what you can identify for sure. If you see or smell mould, throw it all away. Never pull up the whole plant — cut only the tops.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.3

Chamomile: tea and compress

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes
① chamomile flower: white petals, yellow centre ② chamomile tea ③ cool, well-strained tea ④ clean cloth ⑤ cloth on a closed eye, 10 minutes.
Why: Chamomile grows almost everywhere in spring. Traditionally it is drunk for a calm stomach and sleep, and used in compresses.
What you need
  • Chamomile flowers (dried or fresh)
  • Cup and saucer
  • Clean bowl
  • Clean cloths or gauze
  • Strainer or cloth
Step by step
  1. Pick the flowers when the white petals are open. Dry them in the shade.
  2. For tea, put 1–2 teaspoons of flowers in 250 ml hot water.
  3. Cover 10 minutes, strain, and drink warm, especially in the evening.
  4. For a compress, make fresh tea and strain it very well through cloth.
  5. Let it become lukewarm or cool. Never hot on skin or eyes.
  6. Wet a clean cloth, squeeze it, and lay it on closed eyes or irritated skin for 10 minutes.
  7. Use a different cloth for each eye. Throw away leftover tea.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: True chamomile has a hollow yellow centre and smells sweet, like apple. Cut one in half to check.
⚠ Careful: It can cause allergy in people allergic to the daisy family (e.g. ragweed). Ask a doctor if pregnant or taking blood thinners or sedatives. If an eye hurts, is very red, has pus, or vision is blurred, see a doctor at once. If not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor or pharmacist.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.4

Sage and thyme for sore throat and cough

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 15 minutes + 2 weeks
① sage leaves ② glass of lukewarm tea for gargling ③ thyme sprigs ④ jar: thyme covered with honey ⑤ teaspoon.
Why: Sage and thyme grow on every Greek hillside. Traditionally they are used for sore throat and cough.
What you need
  • Dried sage
  • Dried or fresh thyme
  • Salt
  • Honey
  • Glass jar
  • Glass and spoon
Step by step
  1. For a gargle, put 1 teaspoon sage in 250 ml hot water, covered, 10 minutes.
  2. Strain, add a pinch of salt and let it become lukewarm.
  3. Gargle a mouthful for 30 seconds and spit it out. Do not swallow it.
  4. Repeat 3–4 times a day.
  5. For cough syrup, fill a jar halfway with thyme.
  6. Cover it completely with honey and stir to remove air bubbles.
  7. Close it and leave it for 2 weeks. Turn it upside down every day.
  8. Take 1 teaspoon when coughing, up to 3–4 times a day.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: If in a hurry, drink warm thyme tea with a teaspoon of honey. It works the same day.
⚠ Careful: NEVER give honey to babies under 1 year — risk of botulism (serious poisoning). Do not drink a lot of sage for many days. No sage in pregnancy, breastfeeding or epilepsy. See a doctor at once for trouble breathing or swallowing, high fever or blood in the cough. If not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.5

Mountain tea, linden and mint

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 10 minutes
① mountain tea with its flower spike ② linden: flowers under a pale wing ③ mint ④ covered teapot, 5–10 minutes. The moon: linden is for the evening.
Why: Three favourite Greek teas. Traditionally they are drunk for colds, a calm stomach and good sleep.
What you need
  • Mountain tea (dried stems)
  • Linden (dried flowers with their pale wing)
  • Mint (fresh or dried)
  • Teapot or small pot
  • Honey, lemon (optional)
Step by step
  1. For mountain tea, break 2–3 stems with their flowers.
  2. Put them in 500 ml water and simmer 5 minutes. It is for colds.
  3. For linden, put 1 tablespoon of flowers in 250 ml hot water.
  4. Cover 10 minutes. Drink it in the evening for calm and sleep.
  5. For mint, put 5–6 fresh leaves in 250 ml hot water, covered, 5 minutes.
  6. Drink it after meals for a heavy stomach.
  7. Strain. Add honey and lemon once the tea has cooled a little.
  8. Drink 1–3 cups a day, not for months on end.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Mint grows easily in a pot from one sprig rooted in water. Give it its own pot — it spreads.
⚠ Careful: Mountain tea is protected in many areas: do not pick it wild; grow or buy it. No mint for babies and small children; it may worsen heartburn. If pregnant, with heart disease or taking medicines, ask a doctor. No honey under 1 year. If a cold is not better in 2–3 days or the fever is high, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.6

Calendula salve with olive oil and beeswax

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 4 weeks + 1 hour
① calendula flower ② jar: dried flowers covered with oil ③ pot of hot water (water bath) ④ bowl of oil and beeswax pieces ⑤ low fire ⑥ small jars ⑦ test on a cold spoon.
Why: Beeswax salve is the old home ointment. Traditionally it is used on cracked hands, dry skin and small scrapes.
What you need
  • Dried calendula (pot marigold) flowers
  • 200 ml olive oil
  • 25 g beeswax
  • Glass jar
  • Pot and bowl for a water bath
  • Small clean jars
Step by step
  1. Fill a jar halfway with DRIED calendula flowers.
  2. Cover them with olive oil, two fingers above the flowers.
  3. Leave 4 weeks in a warm, shady place. Shake it every day.
  4. Strain the oil through cloth and squeeze well.
  5. Put 200 ml oil and 25 g beeswax in a bowl set in a pot of water (water bath).
  6. Warm on low heat until the wax melts. Stir.
  7. Put a drop on a cold spoon. If too soft, add a little more wax.
  8. Pour into the small jars and let set uncovered. Then close them.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Kept cool it lasts about 1 year. If it smells rancid, throw it away.
⚠ Careful: Dried flowers only: water in fresh ones brings mould. Oil and wax catch fire — never directly on the flame, only a water bath. Test a little on a small patch of skin first (daisy-family allergy). Not for deep or infected wounds or fresh burns. If a wound gets red, swollen or does not close in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.7

St John's wort oil (red oil)

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 40 days
① St John's wort with yellow five-petal flowers ② clear jar: flowers in olive oil ③ sun for about 40 days ④ straining through cloth in a funnel ⑤ dark bottle.
Why: Red St John's wort oil was in every village home. Traditionally it is used on small burns once cooled, scrapes and sore muscles.
What you need
  • Flowering tops of St John's wort (yellow flowers, June)
  • Olive oil
  • Clear glass jar
  • Clean cloth and funnel
  • Dark bottle
Step by step
  1. Pick the yellow flowering tops on a dry day, around late June.
  2. Spread them on a cloth in the shade for 1 day to wilt a little.
  3. Fill the jar loosely with the flowers.
  4. Cover them fully with olive oil. Nothing should stick out of the oil.
  5. Put the jar in the sun for about 40 days. Shake it every day.
  6. The oil turns deep red. Then strain it through a cloth.
  7. Keep it in a dark bottle, in a cool place, up to 1 year.
  8. Put a few drops on a small, clean burn that is already cooled, or a scrape.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The right plant: rub a yellow bud — it stains your fingers red. Against the light, the leaves show tiny see-through dots.
⚠ Careful: For OUTSIDE use ONLY — do not drink it. Taken by mouth, St John's wort interacts with many medicines (birth control pills, blood thinners, antidepressants, heart drugs). It makes skin sensitive to sunlight: do not go into the sun with oil on the skin. Not on a fresh burn before cooling it with water, nor on open blisters or deep wounds. If it goes mouldy, throw it away. If not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor or pharmacist.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.8

Honey on small wounds; garlic and onion

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 5 minutes
① jar of clean honey ② thin layer of honey on a small, clean wound ③ clean plaster on top ④ garlic (in food only) ⑤ sliced onion ⑥ jar: onion and honey for cough.
Why: Honey keeps for years without spoiling. Traditionally it goes on small wounds, and garlic and onion go in food for colds.
What you need
  • Clean honey
  • Boiled water, cooled
  • Clean gauze or plaster
  • Garlic
  • Onion
  • Small jar
Step by step
  1. Wash your hands. Rinse the wound well with clean, boiled water.
  2. With a clean spoon, spread a thin layer of honey on the small wound.
  3. Cover with clean gauze or a plaster.
  4. Change honey and gauze once a day, always with clean hands.
  5. For colds, eat 1–2 cloves of chopped raw garlic in food.
  6. For cough syrup, slice 1 onion and put it in a jar.
  7. Cover with honey, leave 8–12 hours, and take 1 teaspoon of the liquid.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Onion syrup keeps 2–3 days in the fridge or a cold place. Make a little at a time.
⚠ Careful: NEVER give honey to babies under 1 year, by mouth or on a wound. DO NOT put raw garlic on the skin — it can burn it. Only for small, shallow wounds. A deep wound, animal bite, rusty nail or bleeding that will not stop needs a doctor. If it gets red, swollen, more painful, has pus, you get fever, or it is not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.9

Oxymel (vinegar and honey)

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 10 minutes + 2 weeks
① vinegar ② honey ③ dried herbs (optional) ④ 1 part vinegar ⑤ 2 parts honey ⑥ baking paper under the lid ⑦ 1 tablespoon in a glass of water.
Why: Oxymel has been drunk since ancient times. Vinegar and honey preserve herbs without a fridge and make a soothing drink for colds.
What you need
  • Vinegar (apple or wine)
  • Honey
  • Dried thyme, sage or oregano (optional)
  • Glass jar
  • Baking paper
  • Glass of water
Step by step
  1. If you want herbs, fill the jar one third with dried herbs.
  2. Pour in 1 part vinegar, e.g. 1 cup.
  3. Add 2 parts honey, e.g. 2 cups, and stir well.
  4. Put baking paper under the metal lid, because vinegar eats metal.
  5. Leave it 2 weeks in a shady place. Shake it every day.
  6. Strain out the herbs and keep it closed. It lasts months.
  7. Stir 1 tablespoon into a glass of water, warm or cold, and drink.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Without herbs, mixed with cold water, it is the old summer drink of harvest workers.
⚠ Careful: Always diluted in water: neat vinegar harms teeth, throat and stomach. Rinse your mouth after. Not if you have an ulcer or heartburn. No honey for babies under 1 year. Take care with diabetes (it is sugary). If not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.10

Home oral rehydration solution for diarrhoea

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 5 minutes
① 1 litre clean water (boiled, cooled) ② 6 level teaspoons sugar ③ half a level teaspoon salt ④ stir until dissolved ⑤ small sips often.
Why: Diarrhoea drains water and salts from the body — that is the real danger, especially for children and the elderly. This simple drink saves lives.
What you need
  • 1 litre clean water (boiled and cooled)
  • Sugar
  • Salt
  • Teaspoon
  • Jug and spoon
Step by step
  1. Boil the water and let it cool. Measure exactly 1 litre.
  2. Add 6 LEVEL teaspoons of sugar (level, not heaped).
  3. Add half a LEVEL teaspoon of salt. No more.
  4. Stir well until dissolved.
  5. Taste: it should be no saltier than tears.
  6. Take small sips often. After each loose stool, one glass (child: half).
  7. If there is vomiting, wait 10 minutes and start again more slowly.
  8. Make it fresh every day. Throw away what is left after 24 hours.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Keep breastfeeding and keep eating (rice, potato, banana, soup). Food helps the gut heal.
⚠ Careful: Measure carefully: too much salt is dangerous, especially for babies. Get medical help AT ONCE if: there is blood in the stool, high fever, vomiting everything, no urine for 6 hours (baby) or 8 hours (adult), very sleepy or confused, sunken eyes, or a baby under 6 months. If not better in 2 days, find a doctor or pharmacist.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.11

Cleaning teeth without toothpaste

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 3 minutes, twice a day
① olive or mastic twig ② chewed end like a small brush ③ a little soda or salt ④ clean cloth on a finger ⑤ thread between the teeth.
Why: Toothache without a dentist is real misery. Daily cleaning prevents it, even without toothpaste.
What you need
  • Thin olive or mastic twig
  • Baking soda or fine salt
  • Clean small cloth
  • Clean thread (cotton or silk)
  • Water
Step by step
  1. Cut a fresh twig, finger-long and a bit thinner than a pencil.
  2. Peel the end and chew it until it looks like a small brush.
  3. Rub each tooth from the gum downwards, front and back.
  4. Or wrap a cloth round your finger, wet it and dip in a little soda or salt.
  5. Rub teeth and gums gently in small circles.
  6. Pass thread between each pair of teeth, gently, down to the gum.
  7. Rinse your mouth with lightly salted water. Do it morning and night.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Rub the thread on a little beeswax: it slides more easily and does not fray.
⚠ Careful: NEVER use an oleander twig — it is highly poisonous. Use only a tree you know for sure. Do not scrub hard with soda or salt every day for months; they wear the enamel. Do not swallow them. A swollen face, fever, or pain not gone in 2–3 days needs a doctor or dentist.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.12

Keeping mosquitoes, fleas and lice away

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: A few minutes a day
① basil at the window, the mosquito leaves ② bunch of lavender ③ little bag of dried lavender ④ herb smoke, outdoors only ⑤ fine-tooth comb ⑥ bowl of water and vinegar.
Why: Without sprays and chemist products, insects become a big nuisance and can spread disease. The old folk had simple ways.
What you need
  • Pots of basil
  • Lavender (fresh or dried)
  • Cloth for little bags
  • Clay dish and dry herbs
  • Fine-tooth comb (lice comb)
  • Vinegar and water
Step by step
  1. Every 2–3 days empty all standing water: buckets, saucers, hoses. Mosquitoes breed there.
  2. Put pots of basil on window sills and a mosquito net over the bed.
  3. Put little bags of dried lavender in cupboards and under the pillow.
  4. Outdoors in the evening, slowly smoulder dry herbs on a clay dish. The smoke keeps mosquitoes off.
  5. For fleas, wash blankets and bedding in very hot water and shake them in the sun. Sweep every day.
  6. For lice, wet the hair and add a little oil or conditioner.
  7. Comb each lock from root to tip with the fine comb. Wipe the comb on paper.
  8. Rinse with 1 part vinegar to 2 parts water. Repeat every 3–4 days for 2 weeks.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The strongest weapon against mosquitoes is not a herb but an empty bucket.
⚠ Careful: Smoke ONLY outdoors, never in a closed room (carbon monoxide, fire). Never leave a fire unattended. Do not put neat essential oils on skin, on babies or on cats (they are toxic to cats). Vinegar stings the eyes. If bites swell a lot, or you get fever or trouble breathing, find a doctor at once. If not better in 2–3 days, ask a pharmacist.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.13

Olive oil soap (cold process)

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 2 hours + 6–8 weeks
① goggles and gloves ② cold water in a heat-proof jug ③ soda goes INTO the water ④ fumes — outdoors, do not breathe them ⑤ pouring soda water into the oil ⑥ stirring until it thickens ⑦ mould ⑧ bars curing on a shelf 6–8 weeks.
Why: Soap and water prevent many illnesses. With olive oil and caustic soda you can make good soap that lasts for months.
What you need
  • 1000 g olive oil
  • 128 g caustic soda (pure sodium hydroxide)
  • 300 g cold water
  • Goggles, rubber gloves, long sleeves
  • Kitchen scale
  • Stainless pot and heat-proof jug (NOT aluminium)
  • Wooden spoon, thermometer, mould
Step by step
  1. Put on goggles and gloves. Work outdoors or with windows open, no children or pets nearby.
  2. Weigh 300 g cold water into the jug.
  3. Slowly add the 128 g of caustic soda INTO the water. Never water onto soda. Stir.
  4. It gets very hot and gives off fumes: do not breathe them. Let it cool to 40 °C.
  5. Warm the oil to 40 °C and slowly pour in the soda water, stirring.
  6. Keep stirring until it thickens like custard and leaves a trail (can take 1 hour).
  7. Pour into the mould, cover with a towel and leave 1–2 days.
  8. Cut into bars and leave on an airy shelf 6–8 weeks before use.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Always weigh with a scale, not cups. If you change the oil, recalculate the soda.
⚠ Careful: Caustic soda burns skin and eyes and can blind. If it touches skin, rinse with lots of running water for 15 minutes. If it gets in an eye, rinse 15–20 minutes and get to a doctor AT ONCE. If swallowed, do not make the person vomit; doctor at once. Keep the soda locked up, labelled, away from children. Fresh soap burns: wait the full weeks.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.14

Cleaning and disinfecting without shop products

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: Every day
① boiling cloths for 10 minutes ② sun ③ bedding in sun and air ④ bucket of diluted bleach ⑤ bleach: 20 ml in 1 litre of water ⑥ NEVER bleach together with vinegar.
Why: In hard times illness spreads through dirty hands, cloths and worktops. Boiling water, sunshine and a little bleach do wonders.
What you need
  • Large pot
  • Vinegar
  • Wood ash (not from charcoal or painted wood)
  • Household bleach (about 5%)
  • Bucket, gloves, teaspoon
Step by step
  1. Boil dish cloths, kitchen towels and baby dummies for 10 minutes.
  2. Hang bedding, pillows and clothes in the sun. Turn them at midday.
  3. Remove limescale and grease with equal parts vinegar and water. Vinegar cleans but is not a strong disinfectant.
  4. For greasy pots, scrub with damp wood ash, wearing gloves. Rinse well.
  5. To disinfect, put 4 teaspoons (20 ml) bleach in 1 litre of water.
  6. First wash with soap, then wipe with the solution. Leave it 10 minutes to work.
  7. Make fresh solution every day, in cold water, with windows open.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: The cheapest disinfectant: soap and water on hands for 20 seconds, always before eating and after the toilet.
⚠ Careful: NEVER mix bleach with vinegar, acids, ammonia or other cleaners — it makes poisonous gas. Bleach burns eyes and skin: wear gloves. Keep everything closed, labelled, away from children. Wet ash becomes caustic: wear gloves and keep it out of eyes. If someone swallows a cleaner, do not make them vomit; find a doctor at once.
🌿 Herbs & Home Care · 7.15

Aloe and cool water for minor burns

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 20–30 minutes
① cool running water for 20 minutes ② basin ③ potted aloe ④ cut leaf: clear gel only ⑤ burn bigger than the palm = doctor.
Why: Small burns are common around the stove and the fire. The right first step makes a big difference to pain and scarring.
What you need
  • Cool clean water (not ice-cold)
  • Basin or jug
  • Leaf from a potted aloe
  • Clean knife
  • Clean cling film or a clean cloth
Step by step
  1. At once put the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
  2. Remove rings, watch and tight clothes before swelling. Do not pull off anything stuck.
  3. Do not use ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or yoghurt.
  4. Cut a thick aloe leaf at the base and stand it upright 10 minutes to drain the yellow sap.
  5. Rinse it, slit it open and take only the clear gel.
  6. Spread a thin layer of gel on a small, shallow burn, with no open blisters.
  7. Cover loosely with clean cling film or cloth. Do not burst blisters.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: A pot of aloe on the kitchen window sill needs almost no watering and is always ready.
⚠ Careful: Find a DOCTOR if: the burn is bigger than the person's palm, is on the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, is deep, white or black, is from electricity or chemicals, or the person is a baby, child or elderly. Do not eat aloe; the yellow sap irritates. If it gets red, swollen, has pus or is not better in 2–3 days, find a doctor.
Chapter 8

Tools, Rope & Clothes

A sharp knife, a good rope and sturdy clothes are worth a lot when there are no shops. Here you learn to make and mend the things our grandparents never threw away. Start with knots and sewing: you will need them every day.
  1. Sharpening a knife on a stone
  2. Sharpening an axe and splitting wood safely
  3. Replacing a broken handle with a wooden wedge
  4. Four knots for everything
  5. Knots to tighten a load
  6. Rope from plant fibres or plastic bags
  7. Weaving a simple basket
  8. Hand sewing and sewing on a button
  9. Patching torn clothes and trousers
  10. Darning socks and knitwear
  11. Knitting basics: your first scarf
  12. Repairing shoes and tyre-rubber sandals
  13. A broom from heather or sorghum
  14. Pine resin glue (pitch)
  15. Carving a wooden spoon or bowl
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.1

Sharpening a knife on a stone

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 15–20 minutes
① Stone (seen from above) ② Wet cloth underneath ③ Angle about 20° ④ Burr on the edge (magnified) ⑤ Stroke: edge first, heel to tip
Why: A dull knife slips and cuts fingers. A sharp one does the work with little force.
What you need
  • Whetstone, or a smooth, flat river stone
  • Water
  • A wet cloth
  • A piece of leather (e.g. an old belt)
Step by step
  1. Wet the stone and set it on a wet cloth so it will not slide.
  2. If it is a river stone, rub it flat on concrete first.
  3. Hold the blade upright (90°). Tilt it halfway (45°), then halfway again: about 20°.
  4. Push the blade edge-first, as if slicing a thin layer off the stone. Go from heel to tip.
  5. Make 10–15 strokes on one side, keeping the same angle.
  6. Feel the other side for a burr (a thin lip of metal). Move your thumb from spine to edge, never along it.
  7. When the burr runs the whole length, turn the knife and do the same.
  8. Finish with light strokes, one per side. Then pull it on the leather, spine first.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Test: if it slices a sheet of paper cleanly without tearing, it is ready.
⚠ Careful: Keep fingers behind the edge. Never test the edge by running a finger along it. Sharpen sitting down at a steady table.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.2

Sharpening an axe and splitting wood safely

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 30 minutes
① File, pushed toward the eye ② The bevel (the shiny strip) ③ Chopping block ④ Upright log with a crack ⑤ Clear space around you
Why: An axe gives you firewood for heat and cooking. A dull axe bounces off and causes injuries.
What you need
  • Coarse metal file
  • Whetstone
  • Leather gloves
  • A wide chopping block
  • Strong closed shoes
Step by step
  1. Fix the axe firmly, with the blade out past the edge of the bench.
  2. Wear gloves. Push the file from the edge toward the eye, at the old angle. Same strokes on both sides.
  3. Finish with the stone in small circles until the burr is gone.
  4. Clear space around you: two axe lengths, no people or animals near.
  5. Stand the log upright on the chopping block, never on the soil.
  6. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Aim at a crack.
  7. Strike the middle or the far half. If you miss, the axe hits the block, not your leg.
  8. If it sticks, do not yank it. Drive a wooden wedge into the crack.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Wipe a little oil on the steel after work so it does not rust.
⚠ Careful: Never in sandals, when tired, or with children nearby. If the head is loose on the handle, stop and fix it first.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.3

Replacing a broken handle with a wooden wedge

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2–3 hours
① Slot in the top of the handle ② Wooden wedge (hammered down) ③ Hammer head, cut-away view ④ Cut flush with the head
Why: A hammer or axe head lasts a lifetime, but the wooden handle breaks. Replace it and the tool lives again.
What you need
  • Dry hardwood: ash, beech or oak
  • Saw, knife or rasp
  • Drill or iron punch to remove the old wood
  • Hammer
  • Linseed or other oil
Step by step
  1. Saw off the old wood close to the head. Drill or punch out what is left in the eye.
  2. Carve the new handle from straight wood. The grain must run along it.
  3. Shave the top until it fits tightly in the eye. Leave 1 cm sticking out above.
  4. Saw a slot in the top, 2/3 as deep as the eye.
  5. Fit the head. Tap the bottom of the handle on a stump so the head slides down.
  6. Make a thin wedge of dry hardwood, as wide as the eye.
  7. Hammer the wedge into the slot until it will not go further.
  8. Saw off the extra flush with the head. Oil the wood.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Do not soak the tool in water to tighten it: it swells for a few days, then gets looser. Add a second wedge instead.
⚠ Careful: Never work with a loose head: it can fly off and hit someone. Use wood with no knots or cracks.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.4

Four knots for everything

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour of practice
① Reef knot ② Bowline ③ Clove hitch on a post ④ Sheet bend (thick and thin rope)
Why: With four knots you can tie almost anything: bundles, tents, boats, buckets. A good knot holds well and unties easily.
What you need
  • Two ropes, 1 m each (one thick, one thin)
  • A post or rail
Step by step
  1. Reef knot: right over left and under. Then left over right and under.
  2. Bowline (a loop that does not tighten): make a small loop (the "hole") in the rope, end side on top.
  3. Bring the end up through the hole. Take it round behind the rope and back down the hole. Pull tight.
  4. Clove hitch: wrap the rope round the post and cross over itself in an X.
  5. Wrap once more and tuck the end under the X.
  6. Sheet bend: make a U with the thick rope. Pass the thin one up through it.
  7. Wrap the thin rope round the whole U and tuck it under itself. Pull tight.
  8. Always leave a tail of at least 10 cm, and tighten well before loading.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: For the bowline: "the rabbit comes out of the hole, runs round the tree and goes back down the hole."
⚠ Careful: The reef knot slips under load or with ropes of different sizes: use it only for bundles. To pull a person, use only the bowline, round the chest under the arms.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.5

Knots to tighten a load

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour of practice
① Two wraps inside the loop ② One wrap outside, higher up ③ Peg ④ Fixed loop ⑤ Hook or rail ⑥ Pull down
Why: A rope that goes slack drops the load or the tent. These two knots tighten and adjust without untying.
What you need
  • Rope 4–10 m long, 6–10 mm thick
  • A peg or hook
  • The load or the tent
Step by step
  1. Tent-line hitch: pass the rope round the peg and bring the end back up.
  2. Wrap the end twice round the tight line, inside the loop.
  3. Make one more wrap higher up, outside the loop, and pull tight.
  4. Slide the knot up to tighten, down to loosen.
  5. Trucker's hitch: tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, above the load.
  6. Pass the end round the hook or rail below.
  7. Bring the end up through the loop. Pull hard down: it works like a pulley, with double force.
  8. Hold it tight and tie off with two half hitches round both lines.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: An easy middle loop: fold the rope and tie a simple overhand knot with the fold.
⚠ Careful: A tight rope that snaps whips like a lash. Do not stand in line with it. On the road, check the load often.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.6

Rope from plant fibres or plastic bags

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour for 2 metres
① The fold ② Twist each strand away from you ③ Lay it over the other ④ Finished two-strand cord ⑤ Bag cut into strips
Why: When the rope runs out, make it from nettle, broom or old bags. Twisting turns weak fibres into strong cord.
What you need
  • Fibres: dry nettle, broom, rushes, lime-tree bark
  • or plastic bags
  • Scissors or knife
  • Water
Step by step
  1. Soak plant fibres for a few minutes to soften them.
  2. Cut bags into strips 2–3 cm wide.
  3. Take a bundle and fold it in two, a little off-centre, so the ends are uneven.
  4. Hold the fold. Twist the top strand away from you (clockwise).
  5. Lay the twisted strand over the other one, toward you (anticlockwise).
  6. Repeat: twist the new top strand, lay it over. Always the same way.
  7. When a strand gets thin, add new fibres 5 cm before it ends and carry on.
  8. Knot the end. For thicker rope, twist three cords together the same way.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Uneven ends at the start mean the joins fall in different places, so the cord has no weak spot.
⚠ Careful: Handle nettles with gloves or once dried. Homemade cord is never for climbing or holding a person's weight.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.7

Weaving a simple basket

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 1 day
① Base: cross of rods ② Spokes spread like a sun, woven over-under ③ Stakes ④ Woven sides ⑤ Rim
Why: Baskets carry harvest, bread, fruit and eggs. Make them free from chaste-tree, willow, reed or bramble.
What you need
  • 8 thick rods, 40–60 cm (the frame)
  • Many thin, long rods (for weaving)
  • Knife and awl
  • Bucket of water
Step by step
  1. Cut rods in winter. If they have dried, soak them 1–2 days.
  2. Split 4 rods in the middle with the knife. Push the other 4 through them as a cross.
  3. Weave a thin rod round the groups of four, over and under, for two rounds.
  4. Spread the spokes one by one, like a sun. Add one more to make an odd number. Weave a 20 cm base.
  5. Push a long rod beside each spoke (the stakes) and bend them upward.
  6. Weave the sides over and under. Press each row down to keep it tight.
  7. At the top, bend each stake behind the next one and tuck it in to make a rim.
  8. Trim the ends and let it dry in the shade.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Work next to the bucket and wet the rods often. Dry rods snap.
⚠ Careful: Brambles need thick gloves. Remove thorns by pulling the rod through a folded cloth. Knife and awl always pointing away from your body.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.8

Hand sewing and sewing on a button

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30 minutes
① Eye of the needle ② Knot at the end ③ Running stitch ④ Back stitch ⑤ Matchstick under the thread ⑥ The button's shank (side view)
Why: New clothes may be hard to find. With a needle and thread you can keep your clothes going for years.
What you need
  • Needles of different sizes
  • Thread (or thread from an unpicked garment)
  • Scissors
  • Pins and a matchstick
  • Thimble
Step by step
  1. Cut thread as long as your arm (50 cm), on a slant. Wet the tip and push it through the eye.
  2. Knot the end: wrap the thread 2–3 times round a finger and roll it off.
  3. Running stitch: go in and out every 3–5 mm in a straight line. For quick sewing.
  4. Back stitch: come up, go back one stitch, come up one stitch ahead. Strong like a machine.
  5. Button: hold it in place with a matchstick on top, between the holes.
  6. Sew 6–8 times through each pair of holes, over the matchstick.
  7. Remove the match. Wind the thread 4–5 times under the button: this is the shank.
  8. Go to the back and finish with 2–3 tiny stitches on top of each other.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Double thread for buttons and trousers, single for thin clothes. Run the thread over beeswax so it does not tangle.
⚠ Careful: Keep needles and pins in a box, away from children. If a needle drops, find it at once with a torch or a magnet.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.9

Patching torn clothes and trousers

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour
① Hole (trim the threads) ② Patch 2–3 cm bigger ③ Edge folded 1 cm under ④ Small slanted stitches all round
Why: Knees and elbows wear through first. One patch saves the whole garment.
What you need
  • Piece of strong cloth (from an old garment)
  • Needle, thread, scissors
  • Pins
  • A piece of cardboard
  • An iron, if you have one
Step by step
  1. Trim the loose threads round the hole.
  2. Slide the cardboard inside the leg so you do not sew the back side too.
  3. Cut a patch 2–3 cm bigger than the hole all round. Round off the corners.
  4. Fold 1 cm of the edges under. Iron it or press with a fingernail.
  5. Pin the patch over the hole, straight with the weave.
  6. Sew all round the edge with small slanted stitches, every 3–4 mm.
  7. Turn the garment inside out. Sew the edges of the hole down onto the patch.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: For an L-shaped tear, first join the edges with close stitches, then put a patch on the inside.
⚠ Careful: A hot iron melts synthetic cloth: test on a hidden spot first. Never leave a hot iron unattended.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.10

Darning socks and knitwear

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 30 minutes
① Mushroom or potato inside the sock ② Vertical threads ③ Weaving across, over-under (with the needle) ④ Small loop at the turn
Why: A hole in the heel becomes a blister and a sore. Darning rebuilds the fabric, like a tiny loom.
What you need
  • Wool or thick thread, same colour
  • Thick, blunt-tipped needle
  • Wooden darning mushroom, or a potato
Step by step
  1. Put the darning mushroom or potato inside the sock, under the hole.
