  2. Start 1 cm outside the hole, in good fabric. No knot: leave a 5 cm tail.
  3. Lay vertical threads across the hole, close together, side by side.
  4. At each turn leave a tiny loop so it does not pull.
  5. Turn and weave across: over one, under one vertical thread.
  6. The next row is the opposite: under where you went over before.
  7. Push the rows close with the needle. Finish 1 cm into good fabric.
  8. Weave the tail into the knit on the inside and cut.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Darn as soon as the knit gets thin, before a hole opens. It is half the work.
⚠ Careful: Do not pull tight: a hard darn rubs the foot and causes blisters. People with diabetes should check their feet daily for rubbing.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.11

Knitting basics: your first scarf

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 week, a little each evening
① Loops on the needle ② Right needle goes in, making an X ③ Wrap the yarn ④ Pull out the new loop ⑤ The finished scarf
Why: Wool keeps you warm even when wet. One ball of yarn becomes a scarf, a hat or socks.
What you need
  • 2 knitting needles, 5–6 mm (or smooth sticks)
  • 100–150 g of wool
  • Scissors and a thick needle
Step by step
  1. Casting on: make a slip knot and put it on a needle.
  2. Loop the yarn round your thumb and slide the loop onto the needle. Make 20–25 loops.
  3. Hold the full needle in your left hand. Push the right needle into the first loop from the front, making an X.
  4. Wrap the yarn round the tip of the right needle, between the two needles.
  5. Pull the new loop out through the old one and let the old one drop off.
  6. Carry on to the end. Swap the needles between hands and start the next row.
  7. This one stitch alone makes a thick, firm fabric. Knit to 150 cm.
  8. Casting off: knit 2 loops, lift the first over the second. Repeat. Pull the yarn through the last one.
💡 Grandma Areti's tip: Count your loops every few rows. If one drops, catch it at once with a safety pin.
⚠ Careful: Do not leave needles on chairs or beds: they stab. Keep yarn away from fire; synthetic yarn melts and sticks to skin.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.12

Repairing shoes and tyre-rubber sandals

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 hours + 1 day to dry
① Loose sole: roughen and glue ② Wrapped with cord for 24 hours ③ Two-needle stitching ④ Sole cut from tyre tread ⑤ Slot for the strap ⑥ Strap between the toes and round the ankle
Why: Without shoes you cannot walk or work. A loose sole can be glued, and an old tyre becomes soles for years.
What you need
  • Shoe glue or contact glue
  • Sandpaper
  • Awl, 2 thick needles, waxed thread
  • Cord
  • Old car tyre and utility knife
Step by step
  1. Clean and dry the sole and the upper. Roughen both with sandpaper.
  2. Spread thin glue on both sides. Wait 10–15 minutes until it no longer sticks to a finger.
  3. Press hard and wrap tightly with cord. Leave it 24 hours.
  4. Leather: punch holes with the awl every 5 mm, 4 mm from the edge.
  5. Sew with two needles, one at each end of the thread. They cross in every hole.
  6. Sandal: stand on the tyre tread and trace your foot, 1 cm wider.
  7. Cut with the utility knife, always away from your body. Make 3 slots for the straps.
  8. Thread a strap or cord: between the toes, round the ankle, and tie.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Choose rubber with no steel wires inside. If wires show at the cut, discard that piece: they stab the foot.
⚠ Careful: Contact glue gives off fumes: work outdoors, away from flames. The knife slips on rubber: wet the blade with soapy water and keep your other hand behind the cut.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.13

A broom from heather or sorghum

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 2 hours
① Stick with notches ② Thick ends of the stems pointing up ③ Tight bindings in 3 places ④ Bottom trimmed straight
Why: A clean house and yard keep mice and disease away. Our grandparents made brooms from heather, broom-corn sorghum or broom.
What you need
  • Dry heather, sorghum or broom (an armful)
  • Straight stick 120–140 cm, 3 cm thick
  • Wire or strong string
  • Knife or pruners
Step by step
  1. Cut the stems in late summer. Dry them 1–2 weeks in the shade.
  2. Strip the leaves from the lower part. Keep the stems straight and the same length.
  3. Cut 2–3 notches round the end of the stick so the binding grips.
  4. Arrange the stems round the stick, thick ends up, 20 cm up the stick.
  5. Bind tightly at the notches: wrap the wire 6–8 times and twist the ends.
  6. Add a second layer of stems outside and bind again 10 cm lower.
  7. Bind a third time round the middle of the brush so it does not spread.
  8. Trim the bottom straight in one cut.
💡 Grandma Maria's tip: Soak the broom in water for an hour before first use. It becomes springy and does not break.
⚠ Careful: Heather and broom catch fire easily: keep the broom away from fireplaces and stoves. Turn wire ends inward so they do not scratch.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.14

Pine resin glue (pitch)

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 hour
① Dry resin on the trunk ② Tin on embers, not flames ③ Charcoal powder ④ Finished "glue stick"
Why: Without shop glue, pine resin sticks, waterproofs and seals. It was used on barrels, boats and tool handles.
What you need
  • Dry pine resin (the drops on the trunk)
  • Charcoal from the fire, crushed to powder
  • A little fine dry grass
  • Old tin (never for food again)
  • Sticks
Step by step
  1. Collect resin drops that have dried on old wounds of the trunk. Do not wound the tree.
  2. Pick out bark and dirt.
  3. Put the resin in the tin over a few embers, not over flames. Melt it slowly.
  4. If it smokes a lot, take it off: it is too hot.
  5. Stir in 1 part charcoal powder to 4 parts resin. Add a pinch of grass.
  6. Test a drop on a stone. If it cracks like glass once cool, add a little fat or beeswax.
  7. Wind the glue onto the end of a stick, like a lollipop, and let it cool.
  8. To use, warm the tip near the fire and smear it on a dry, warm spot.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Keep a "glue stick" in your toolbox. It fixes blades in handles, waterproofs containers and seals cracks.
⚠ Careful: Melted resin catches fire and burns like hot oil. Work outdoors with a lid nearby to smother flames, never water. Keep children away.
🪢 Tools, Rope & Clothes · 8.15

Carving a wooden spoon or bowl

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: half a day
① Spoon drawn on the split wood ② Cut away from your body ③ Thumb pushes the back of the blade ④ Glowing ember ⑤ Blow through a reed
Why: Spoons, ladles and bowls come from a branch. The wood is free, and you learn to use a knife safely.
What you need
  • Green wood with no knots, 30 cm (lime, cherry, willow, poplar)
  • Sharp knife
  • Pencil
  • Embers and a reed for the bowl
  • Sandpaper and food oil
Step by step
  1. Split the branch in two. Draw the spoon on the flat side, away from the pith (the dark centre).
  2. Remove waste wood with small cuts, always outward, away from your body.
  3. Cut with the grain, from thick to thin. If the wood tears, turn it round.
  4. For fine cuts, push the back of the blade with the thumb of your other hand.
  5. Spoon: scoop the hollow with the knife tip, from the edges toward the centre.
  6. Bowl: put a glowing ember in the centre and blow gently through the reed.
  7. Scrape out the burnt wood with a stone or spoon. Add a new ember until it is deep enough.
  8. Let it dry slowly for a week in the shade. Sand it and oil it.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Carve the wood green: it is soft like cheese. Dry wood is like stone.
⚠ Careful: Never cut toward your body, your leg or the holding hand. Never use oleander: it is poisonous. Burn bowls only outdoors, with water nearby.
Chapter 9

Home, Building & Finding your way

Our grandparents built with stone, mud and lime, and found their way by the sun and the stars. In this chapter you learn to make a shelter, keep your home warm and dry, lift heavy loads without machines and read the sky. Simple materials, simple tools, lots of patience.
  1. Quick shelter with a tarp or branches
  2. Insulating windows and doors for winter
  3. Stopping a roof leak temporarily
  4. Building a dry stone wall
  5. Making mud bricks
  6. Lime whitewash and lime mortar
  7. Well windlass, lever and pulley
  8. A-frame level for contour lines on a slope
  9. Small solar power for light and phone charging
  10. Finding north with the sun
  11. Finding north at night: the North Star
  12. Telling time with the sun
  13. Reading the weather without forecasts
  14. Moon phases and the farmer's year
  15. Carrying an injured person: improvised stretcher
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.1

Quick shelter with a tarp or branches

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 30–60 minutes
Left, lean-to (side view): ① pole in a forked stick ② tarp at a slant ③ peg ④ bed of leaves; the red arrow is the wind. Right, A-frame: ⑤ rope between two trees ⑥ peg.
Why: Cold, rain and wind kill faster than hunger. A simple cover keeps you dry and warm.
What you need
  • tarp about 3×3 m (or many leafy branches)
  • 10 m of rope
  • 1 straight pole 2–3 m
  • 6–8 small pegs or stones
  • dry leaves or pine needles
Step by step
  1. Pick a flat, dry spot that is sheltered from the wind.
  2. Lean-to: tie the pole level between two trees or forked sticks, at waist height.
  3. Throw the tarp over the pole and bring it down at a slant to the ground.
  4. Turn the closed back towards the wind. Peg the edges or hold them with stones.
  5. A-frame (like a tent): stretch a rope between two trees, throw the tarp over it, peg both sides.
  6. No tarp: lean sticks on the pole and cover them with branches, bottom to top, like roof tiles.
  7. Lay leaves 20 cm thick inside. The ground pulls the heat out of you.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Make it steep: the steeper the tarp, the faster the rain runs off.
⚠ Careful: Do not pitch under dead hanging branches or in a dry stream bed (sudden floods). Keep fire at least 2 m from the tarp. Never use charcoal or a gas stove inside a closed shelter: carbon monoxide.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.2

Insulating windows and doors for winter

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 afternoon
① clear plastic stretched on the frame ② thick blanket as a curtain ③ felt strip round the door ④ sand-filled draft snake; the red arrow is the cold draft being stopped.
Why: Without power or fuel, heat is precious. Most cold gets in through glass and gaps.
What you need
  • clear plastic sheet
  • tape or drawing pins
  • thick blankets
  • old trousers or a sock
  • sand or rice
  • strips of felt or an old towel
Step by step
  1. Find the drafts: hold a lit candle near doors and windows. Where it flickers, air is coming in.
  2. Stretch plastic over the window frame, on the inside. The air gap works like double glazing.
  3. Hang a thick blanket as a curtain. Close it at night, open it by day to let the sun in.
  4. Nail a strip of felt or towel all round the door frame.
  5. Make a draft snake: fill a trouser leg with sand, tie the ends, lay it under the door.
  6. Close the rooms you do not use. Heat only one.
  7. Lay rugs or blankets on the floor.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Grandma also hung a blanket behind the front door. The hallway became a buffer that kept the cold out.
⚠ Careful: Always leave some fresh air when a stove, fireplace or gas heater burns. Never use a charcoal brazier in a closed room: carbon monoxide has no smell and kills in sleep. Keep an exit clear in case of fire.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.3

Stopping a roof leak temporarily

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 hours
① tarp over the ridge ② sandbags (or a batten) at the edges ③ bucket under the drip ④ string guiding the drip.
Why: Water that gets in rots wood, spoils food and brings mould. A tarp saves the house until a proper repair.
What you need
  • bucket, string
  • large tarp
  • sandbags or 2 wooden battens
  • hammer, nails
  • spare tile or a piece of sheet metal
  • ladder and a helper
Step by step
  1. Inside: put a bucket under the drip. Hang a string from the drip to the bucket so it does not splash.
  2. Move things out from below and mop up the water at once.
  3. Wait until rain and wind stop. Climb only on a dry roof.
  4. Find the broken or slipped tile. Water often enters higher up than the drip.
  5. Fit a new tile or slide sheet metal under the tiles above.
  6. For big damage: throw the tarp over the ridge and bring it down past the damage.
  7. Weigh the edges with sandbags tied in pairs, or roll the edge round a batten and nail it.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Always take the tarp over the ridge. Otherwise water runs underneath it.
⚠ Careful: A fall from a roof can kill. Never in rain, wind, on wet tiles or alone. Step over the beams, not the middle of tiles. Stay away from power lines.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.4

Building a dry stone wall

Difficulty: ●●●
Time: 1 day for 2–3 metres
Left, cross-section: ① big base stones in the trench ② each face leans inwards ③ hearting with small stones ④ through stone ⑤ cap stones. Right, front view: ⑥ cap; every stone sits on two.
Why: Dry stone walls hold terraces, animal pens and fields for centuries. They need only stones, hands and patience.
What you need
  • many stones (about 1 tonne per 1 m of wall, 1 m high)
  • pickaxe, shovel
  • thick gloves
  • string and 4 stakes
  • lump hammer
Step by step
  1. Sort the stones: big for the base, long ones as through stones, flat for the top, small for filling.
  2. Dig a trench 15–20 cm down to firm soil. Base about 70 cm wide for a 1 m wall.
  3. Lay the biggest stones in the base, long side going into the wall.
  4. Build both faces together. Each face leans in about 10–15 cm per metre of height. Use the string.
  5. Place 'one on two': each stone covers the joint below. Never joint over joint.
  6. Pack the middle tightly with small stones. No stone should wobble.
  7. At half height lay long stones that cross from face to face, one every 1 m.
  8. Finish with flat cap stones on top, upright or slanted, tying both faces together.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Lift each stone only once: look first, then lift. If it does not sit, turn it, do not force it.
⚠ Careful: Lift with your legs, back straight. Gloves and closed shoes protect fingers and toes. Without experience, stay below 1.2 m, and never build walls that hold up a road or a house.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.5

Making mud bricks

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 day + 3–4 weeks drying
① pit for treading the mud ② chopped straw ③ wooden mould on flat ground ④ the mould seen from above (no bottom) ⑤ bricks drying on edge ⑥ a fresh brick lying flat for the first days.
Why: With soil, straw and water people built houses, ovens and sheds. The material is under your feet.
What you need
  • soil with clay (sticky when wet)
  • sand
  • straw cut to 5–10 cm
  • water
  • bottomless wooden mould, inside about 30×15×10 cm
  • shovel, buckets
Step by step
  1. Test the soil: roll a pencil-thick snake. If it bends without cracking, it has enough clay.
  2. Mix about 1 part soil with 1 part sand. If the soil is sandy, use less sand.
  3. Add water and tread with your feet, like grape treading, until it is like stiff dough.
  4. Add straw, about 1 bucket for every 4 buckets of mud, and tread again.
  5. Wet the mould. Put it on flat, sanded ground, fill it, press the corners, level the top.
  6. Lift the mould straight up. The brick stays on the ground.
  7. Leave it flat 2–3 days, then stand it on edge. Cover it from rain.
  8. After 3–4 weeks test it: drop it from waist height onto soil. If it does not break, it is ready.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Make 3–4 test bricks with different mixes first. If they crack, add more sand or straw.
⚠ Careful: Greece has earthquakes: do not build a house for people without an engineer. Mud bricks are fine for an oven, a shed, a low garden wall. They need a solid stone base and a good roof, because water melts them.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.6

Lime whitewash and lime mortar

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1 day (+ 2 weeks to mature)
① add lime into the water, slowly ② metal bucket (it gets hot and boils) ③ goggles ④ rubber glove, long sleeve ⑤ wide brush ⑥ fresh whitewash.
Why: Lime disinfects, keeps the house cool, keeps insects away and binds stones. That is why our villages were white.
What you need
  • slaked lime putty or quicklime powder
  • metal bucket
  • goggles, rubber gloves, long sleeves
  • wide brush
  • coarse salt
  • sand (for mortar)
  • clean water for rinsing
Step by step
  1. Put on goggles and gloves before opening the lime. Keep children and animals away.
  2. If you have quicklime: put 3 parts water in the bucket and slowly add 1 part lime to it. Never water onto lime.
  3. It will boil and steam by itself. Stir with a long stick, from a distance.
  4. Cover it and leave it 2 weeks to mature into putty, under a little water.
  5. Whitewash: thin the putty with water until it is like milk. Add a handful of salt per bucket.
  6. Wet the wall. Brush on thin coats, 3–4 times, in the shade. Let each coat dry.
  7. Mortar: mix 1 part putty with 3 parts sand. Keep the wall damp 3–4 days so it sets.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Thin coats, not thick. Thick whitewash peels. Whitewash every spring.
⚠ Careful: Lime burns skin and can blind. If it gets in the eyes: rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and see a doctor at once. Slaking gives off great heat and splashes. Do not store it in thin plastic or near food.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.7

Well windlass, lever and pulley

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 1–2 days
① drum (log) ② crank ③ rope ④ bucket ⑤ pivot stone ⑥ heavy stone being lifted ⑦ push down the long end ⑧ pulley.
Why: Without pumps or cranes, only old-time mechanics lift water and loads. Small force, big work.
What you need
  • log 15–20 cm thick for the drum
  • 2 strong posts
  • Z-shaped iron crank
  • strong rope, bucket
  • long strong pole or crowbar
  • pulley wheel
Step by step
  1. Set two posts at the sides of the well, buried deep or tied to the well wall.
  2. Lay the log across them so it turns in notches or iron rings.
  3. Fix the crank on one end. A crank arm of 30–40 cm makes the load 4–5 times lighter.
  4. Tie the rope firmly to the drum and the bucket to the other end. Turn to wind it up.
  5. Lever: put a stone (the pivot) very close to the load. Push down the long end.
  6. The closer the pivot is to the load, the easier it lifts. Wedge it up with wood bit by bit.
  7. Pulley: hang it high on a strong beam. You pull down, using your body weight.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Add a wedge or ratchet stop on the drum. If you let go of the crank, the bucket does not fall back.
⚠ Careful: A crank that slips can break arms and teeth. Always cover the well because of children. Never climb down into a well: the air at the bottom can suffocate you. Never stand under a load you are lifting.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.8

A-frame level for contour lines on a slope

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 1 hour to make
① top joint with string ② plumb weight ③ level mark at the middle of the crossbar ④ stakes at the feet ⑤ the contour line of stakes.
Why: For terraces, water channels and trees on a slope, you need level lines on the ground. Then rainwater stays in the field.
What you need
  • 3 straight sticks (two of 2 m, one of 1 m)
  • nails or wire
  • string and a stone as a weight
  • knife or marker
  • many small stakes
Step by step
  1. Tie the two long sticks at the top like an 'A'. Spread the feet about 2 m apart.
  2. Nail the short stick across at half height.
  3. Hang a string with a weight from the top, so it hangs in front of the crossbar.
  4. Stand it on nearly flat ground. Mark where the string crosses.
  5. Turn it round, feet in the same holes. Mark again. Halfway between the two marks is 'level'.
  6. On the slope: put a stake at one foot. Move the other foot up or down until the string hits the mark.
  7. Put a stake there. Move the frame on and repeat. The stakes show the contour line.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Smooth the line by eye; do not follow every small dip. For terraces, one line every 1–2 m of height.
⚠ Careful: On steep slopes take care not to slip. Do not dig channels that send water towards houses or roads.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.9

Small solar power for light and phone charging

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 2–3 hours
① solar panel ② charge controller ③ fuse on the red (+) wire ④ 12 V battery ⑤ 12 V LED lamp ⑥ phone on a USB charger.
Why: Without mains power, a little light at night and a charged phone make a big difference. The sun is free.
What you need
  • 12 V solar panel, 50–100 W
  • 12 V charge controller (small box that protects the battery)
  • 12 V battery (car, or better a deep-cycle one)
  • 10–15 A fuse
  • red and black wire
  • 12 V LED lamp, 12 V USB car charger
Step by step
  1. Face the panel south, tilted about 35–40°, with no shade.
  2. Red is always positive (+), black is negative (−).
  3. Put the fuse in the red wire, close to the battery +.
  4. Connect the battery to the controller FIRST.
  5. Then connect the panel to the controller. A charging light should come on.
  6. Connect the lamp and USB charger to the controller's load output, not straight to the battery.
  7. To disconnect: panel first, then battery.
  8. Do not drain the battery below half (about 12.2 V). It lives much longer.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Wipe the dust off the panel every few days. A dirty panel gives much less.
⚠ Careful: Never touch + to −: sparks, melted wires, fire. The battery holds acid and gives off explosive gas: keep it ventilated, away from flames, wear goggles. House mains (230 V) can kill: do not touch it.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.10

Finding north with the sun

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 20 minutes
Left: ① upright stick ② first stone, West ③ second stone, East ④ North; the red arrow runs West to East. Right: ⑤ hour hand pointing at the sun ⑥ halfway to 12 points South.
Why: Without a phone or compass, the sun tells you where you are going. It works wherever you can see a shadow.
What you need
  • straight stick about 1 m
  • 2 small stones
  • watch with hands (for the second method)
Step by step
  1. Shadow method: push the stick upright into flat ground.
  2. Put a stone at the tip of the shadow. This is West.
  3. Wait 15–20 minutes. Put a second stone at the new shadow tip. This is East.
  4. Stand with the first stone on your left and the second on your right. You are facing North.
  5. Watch method: hold the watch flat. Turn it so the hour hand points at the sun.
  6. Halfway between the hour hand and 12 points South. In summer time, use halfway to 1.
  7. North is straight opposite South.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. At midday in Greece it is always to the south.
⚠ Careful: Never look straight at the sun, not even briefly: it burns the eyes. The watch method is for the northern hemisphere and is only approximate.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.11

Finding north at night: the North Star

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 10 minutes
① Big Dipper (the 'pan') ② the two pointer stars ③ North Star ④ Cassiopeia (W shape); the red line extends the pointers.
Why: The North Star never moves in the sky. It shows North all night, all year.
What you need
  • clear sky
  • a dark place away from lights
  • a little patience for your eyes to adjust (10 minutes)
Step by step
  1. Find the Big Dipper: 7 bright stars shaped like a pan with a handle.
  2. Look at the two stars at the end of the pan, opposite the handle. They are the 'pointers'.
  3. Imagine a line from the lower to the upper one and extend it about 5 times their gap.
  4. There you find a lonely, not very bright star. This is the North Star.
  5. If the Dipper is low or hidden, find Cassiopeia: 5 stars shaped like a W or M.
  6. The North Star is about halfway between Cassiopeia and the Big Dipper.
  7. Below the North Star, on the horizon, is North. Leave a marker for the morning.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Your fist at arm's length is about 10°. In Greece the North Star is about 4 fists above the horizon.
⚠ Careful: Do not walk at night over unknown ground without light: cliffs, holes, wells. Better mark the direction and walk in the morning.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.12

Telling time with the sun

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: 5 minutes – 1 day
Left: ① sun ② horizon ③ fingers from horizon to sun (each finger about 15 minutes). Right: ④ upright stick ⑤ shortest shadow, noon, points North ⑥ stones marking each hour.
Why: How much daylight is left? You must know when to head back or make camp before dark.
What you need
  • your hand
  • straight stick 1 m
  • 10–12 small stones
  • a watch (only once, to set up the sundial)
Step by step
  1. Stretch your arm out, palm towards you, fingers level.
  2. Put your lowest finger on the horizon, below the sun.
  3. Count how many fingers fit up to the sun. Each finger is about 15 minutes to sunset.
  4. One hand (4 fingers) is about 1 hour.
  5. Sundial: push a stick upright in a flat, open place.
  6. When the shadow is shortest, it is sun noon and the shadow points North. In Greece this is about 12:30 in winter, 13:30 in summer.
  7. While you still have a watch, put a stone at the shadow tip every hour.
  8. Redo the marks every 2–3 weeks, because the sun's height changes with the seasons.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: After sunset you get about half an hour of twilight. Do not count on it for work, only for getting back.
⚠ Careful: Never look straight at the sun. Put your fingers below it and look out of the corner of your eye. In mountains the sun 'sets' earlier behind the peaks.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.13

Reading the weather without forecasts

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: a few minutes each day
① high 'horse tail' clouds ② ring around the sun ③ tower cloud with a flat top ④ lightning and rain ⑤ swallow flying low ⑥ red sunset.
Why: Farmers, shepherds and fishermen had to know about rain and storms in advance. The sky gives signs.
What you need
  • your eyes
  • a notebook
  • a strip of cloth tied up high (shows the wind)
Step by step
  1. Thin, high clouds like 'horse tails': weather change in 1–2 days.
  2. A ring (halo) round the sun or moon: rain is coming.
  3. White puffy clouds growing tall in the afternoon, like towers with a flat top: storm in a few hours.
  4. Red sky at night, fair weather tomorrow. Red sky in the morning, take care.
  5. Swallows flying low, strong smell of soil, smoke sinking down: rain is near.
  6. Dew on the grass in the morning: a clear day.
  7. Lightning: count seconds until the thunder. Divide by 3: that many kilometres away.
  8. Write down every day what you saw and what weather came. In a year you will know your place.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Every place has its own signs. Ask the old people of the village: they know them.
⚠ Careful: If thunder comes in less than 30 seconds, get into a house or car at once. Stay away from lone trees, hilltops, water and fences. Do not cross rising streams.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.14

Moon phases and the farmer's year

Difficulty: ●○○
Time: one month of watching
Top, the phases from left to right: ① new moon ② first quarter (light on the right, growing) ③ full moon ④ last quarter (light on the left, shrinking). Bottom, the farmer's year: ⑤ winter, planting trees ⑥ spring, seedlings ⑦ summer, harvest ⑧ autumn, sowing.
Why: The moon was our grandparents' calendar and lamp. At full moon you can walk, work and guard animals without a light.
What you need
  • the sky every evening
  • a notebook or wall calendar
Step by step
  1. The moon's cycle lasts about 29.5 days: new moon, first quarter, full moon, last quarter.
  2. Lit on the right: it is 'growing'. Lit on the left: it is 'shrinking'.
  3. The full moon rises as the sun sets and shines all night. Plan night work then.
  4. A growing moon is seen in the evening, a shrinking one in the morning.
  5. Autumn (Oct–Nov): sow wheat, barley, broad beans, peas, garlic, onions.
  6. Winter (Dec–Feb): plant trees, prune. Potatoes at the end of February.
  7. Spring (Mar–May): put tomato, pepper and courgette seedlings out after the last frost.
  8. Summer: harvest, water. In August sow cabbage and cauliflower for winter.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: Old farmers sowed above-ground crops on a growing moon and root crops on a shrinking moon. It is tradition, not proven: try it yourself.
⚠ Careful: Dates change with altitude: in the mountains sow 2–4 weeks later in spring. Ask local people.
🏡 Home, Building & Finding your way · 9.15

Carrying an injured person: improvised stretcher

Difficulty: ●●○
Time: 10 minutes
Top, stretcher from above: ① poles ② jackets buttoned, poles through the sleeves. Bottom: ③ injured person lying down ④ two people lift together ⑤ the arrow shows the direction, feet first.
Why: When no ambulance comes, you must move someone safely. Two poles and three jackets make a stretcher.
What you need
  • 2 strong straight poles, about 2.2 m
  • 2–3 jackets with buttons or zips (or a blanket)
  • 2–4 people
Step by step
  1. Button up the jackets and turn the sleeves inside.
  2. Push the two poles through the sleeves, one jacket next to the other.
  3. With a blanket: lay it out, put a pole at 1/3, fold over, put the other pole, fold again.
  4. Test it first with a healthy person lying on it.
  5. Lay the injured person on it. Cover them so they do not get cold.
  6. Lift all together, 'one, two, three', bending your knees, back straight.
  7. Walk feet first. Going uphill, head first.
  8. No poles, short distance: two people each grip their own right wrist and the other's left wrist. It makes a 'seat'.
💡 Grandpa Diamantis' tip: The strongest person takes the head end. The front person calls out obstacles: 'step', 'stone', 'stop'.
⚠ Careful: If the neck or back may be hurt, do NOT move them unless there is danger (fire, water, landslide). Call for help (112) if you can. This is not a substitute for a doctor.

Stay strong – and teach this to your children.

✝ Dedicated to the memory of my grandfather, Diamantis.
